The Cropsey legend is the most widespread camp ghost story in northeastern North America. It originated in the New York area and tells of a deranged figure (with a hook hand or axe) who stalks campers. The legend became entangled with real crimes when Andre Rand, a janitor at Willowbrook State School on Staten Island, was convicted of kidnapping children in the 1970s-80s.

The 1981 horror film The Burning and the 2009 documentary Cropsey both draw on the Cropsey camp ghost story legend. The Burning was produced by Harvey and Bob Weinstein and features a camp caretaker named 'Cropsy' burned in a prank gone wrong.

A 2019 Slate article reported that about a third of American summer camps prohibit ghost stories, while the tradition of scary campfire storytelling has been declining. Some camp staff cite concerns over potentially traumatizing children.

The 1935 camp history document casually references 'the haunted house' as a location where campers went on eating-out day, suggesting an established tradition of associating a specific building on or near the camp property with supernatural narratives by 1935.

The Kanawha River in West Virginia, which has a similar name to Kanawana, derives its name from a Shawnee or Delaware word generally believed to mean 'white rocks' or possibly 'new water.' The Kanawha Indian band was a branch of the Algonquin family related to the Nanticokes and Delawares.

No Kanawana-specific ghost stories have been found in any written sources, including the Gas Bag (1923), Green Triangle newsletters (1932-1940), camp brochures, or online alumni accounts. Camp ghost stories are overwhelmingly transmitted as oral tradition.

YMCA camps across North America have a long tradition of campfire storytelling. Camp-specific ghost stories are common, with examples including the 'Mud Lake Monster' and 'Grandpappy' at Camp Minikani, and 'Cropsey' at Camp IHC. These stories often evolve with each retelling.

Quebec folklore traditions relevant to Kanawana campfire culture include La Chasse-Galerie (The Flying Canoe, where lumberjacks make a devil's pact to fly home in a canoe over the Laurentians), Le Loup-Garou (werewolf), and Le Beau Danseur (the devil at the dance). These legends have over 200 versions across Quebec.

The 'Chopsy' ghost story is reportedly told at Camp Kanawana, featuring an ax murderer. No published or online documentation of this specific story name has been found. The name 'Chopsy' does not appear in any indexed web source, folklore archive, academic database, Reddit, or camp ghost story collection as of February 2027. Over 30 web searches using the exact terms 'Chopsy', 'Chopsey', 'Chopsie', and 'Chops' combined with camp/ghost/story/axe keywords returned zero relevant results.

The Cropsey Maniac legend was first academically documented by Haring and Breslerman in a survey of 11 New York City informants conducted in fall 1966, published in New York Folklore 3 (1977), pp. 15-27. Key finding: while all variants had different specific details, all significant plot events went relatively unchanged. The story was always localized to where the informant first heard it.

Documented name variants of the Cropsey character include: George Cropsey (judge/businessman), Jack Cropsey (caretaker/handyman), Judge Cropsey (scout leader), Old Man Cropsey (farmer/escaped prisoner), and Cropsy (film adaptation in The Burning, 1981). The 1982 film Madman changed the name to Madman Marz after discovering The Burning was already using the Cropsey concept.

'Chopsy' is hypothesized to be a Kanawana-specific local adaptation of the widespread 'escaped maniac with an axe' campfire story archetype, following the documented pattern where each camp localizes the story with its own name, setting, and details. The name evokes 'chopping' (with an axe), paralleling Cropsey/Cropsy, Stumpy, and Madman Marz. No direct documentary link between Chopsy and Cropsey has been established. This hypothesis requires oral history confirmation.

The 'Stumpy' ghost story (documented by John Kotula) is another named variant of the camp axe-murderer archetype. Stumpy is a one-armed psycho killer whose arm was severed by an axe accident. He threatens campers with 'I'm going to chop you!' The story has been scaring campers 'for at least half a century' and exists in many versions across many camps.

The 'maniac in the woods' campfire story archetype serves a documented social function at summer camps: it reinforces rules about not wandering into the woods alone at night, builds community through shared fear, and allows counselors to establish authority over campers. Folklorists Leslie Paris, Bill Ellis ('The Camp Mock-Ordeal Theater as Life', 1981), and Jan Harold Brunvand (The Vanishing Hitchhiker, 1981) have all studied these stories as social rituals and cautionary tales.

The Legend of Anson Minor is the most widespread camp ghost story in Ontario. It was documented by folklorist Edith Fowke (York University) in 'The Tale of Anson Minor: An Ontario Camp Legend' (Ethnologies 3:1, 1981, pp. 3-15). Fowke presented multiple previously unpublished versions, questioned the legend's historicity, and described the pattern of camp ghost stories in North America.

The Anson Minor legend tells of a farmer who owned the land where a summer camp now stands. He suffered a gruesome farming accident (leg caught in thresher/plough), lost his leg, fell into ruin, and hanged himself in his barn. His ghost haunts the camp, limping through the fields carrying a green-glowing lantern. The legend is told at camps across Ontario and Nova Scotia, including Camp White Pine and Camp Kadimah.

The Fireside Canada podcast (Episode 35, September 26, 2024, hosted by David Williams) devoted a 38-minute episode to the Legend of Anson Minor, tracing its origins to the original camp that spawned the story and the tragic events that inspired it. The podcast also covers La Chasse-Galerie (Episode 5, 2021) and other Canadian legends.

The Kamp Kanawana Marching Song (also called the Kanawana Cheer) is a call-and-response cheer that includes 'Hail, hail, the gang's all here' as its refrain. It is the most widely known Kanawana cheer. The song's lost verses — originally part of a three-verse song — were rediscovered in the Kanawana Archives at Concordia University in 2006. Only the first verse survives in the modern cheer.

The Kamp Kanawana Marching Song is not original to Kanawana. Its refrain 'Hail, hail, the gang's all here' derives from the 1915 American popular song 'Alabama Jubilee' (music by George L. Cobb, words by Jack Yellen, written under pseudonym D. A. Esrom / Dolly Morse), which was set to a tune originally composed by Arthur Sullivan for the comic opera The Pirates of Penzance. The same refrain is also the origin of the Glasgow Celtic football fight song.

The cheer text from the Spirit of Kanawana blog includes elements such as 'Kamp Kanawana, are you ready?!', call-and-response marching, 'Our camping songs! We're gonna tramp, tramp, tramp on through the rain...', 'So let's sing, sing, sing, siiiinng!', and the camp name spelled out: 'K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A, Kanawana!'

The 1922 camp cheer text in full reads: 'Yo Triumphy! Yo Triumphy! / Hoben Sloben Rebecca Leeammour, / De hoop de hoop de Shalla de Veer, / De boom de rye de hye de pop, / Whooneka Heeneka Waac de Waac, / Hob Dob de Bowl de Bara, / Con Slob de Hob Dob Rah, / Kanawana---Rah!' This is a nonsensical rallying chant typical of early 20th century camp cheers.

The 1923 Gas Bag documents sing-songs as a central evening activity at Kanawana: 'the evenings around the fire with their story-telling and their sing-songs.' Multiple original camp songs with chorus structures were published in the Gas Bag, including 'Sunny, How Long' (a comic song about camp cook 'Sunny') and 'She Told Me So' (a multi-verse comic song). A song set to the tune of 'Yes, We Have No Bananas' (1923 hit) parodied the dining hall ice cream policy.

In the summer of 1923, a 'Sing-Sing Service' was held around the Senior raft in the evening, suggesting a vesper-style group singing event on the water. The same summer featured a Senior 'Dumbell' Revue with a Spanish Dance and other performance elements.

A 'musicale' — a formal musical performance — was held during the eighth week of the 1935 Kanawana season, described as 'a program without precedent in the annals of Kanawana' and 'a fine effort much appreciated by the whole camp.' This is the earliest documented formal musical event at Kanawana.

In 1938, Benny Leshley organized a choir at the outdoor chapel to lead singing. The choir was still recruiting new members as of the July 29, 1938 Green Triangle. Leshley was identified as the organist of Christ Church Cathedral. Guest pianist Brock Brace (a Juvenile camper who also composed) performed in a musicale, playing one of his mother's compositions and taking requests. Sammy Shashley provided regular piano recitals.

The 1922 brochure describes a 'short morning devotional period at the breakfast table' as part of the religious program, along with 'the quiet period before lights out led by the tent leader' and 'Sunday services in the open-air chapel and around the fire.' This morning devotional is the earliest documented reference to a meal-time grace or prayer at Kanawana.

The 1921 and 1922 brochures both list 'musical instruments' and 'music' among items campers should bring to camp, indicating that camper-supplied instruments were part of the camp music culture from at least 1921.

The Concordia Archives (P145/12B07 Program sub-series) contain: song sheets and skits from 1925 and 1927; Kanawana song books from 1941-1945; and a Canadian YMCA song book from 1941-1945. These are the only documented Kanawana-specific song collections in any known archive.

The Concordia Archives (P145/12B04 Communications sub-series) contain radio broadcasts for Kamp Kanawana promotion from 1936-1941, broadcast on Station CFCF Montreal. The June 26, 1941 broadcast transcript is digitized on the Internet Archive. CFCF (Canadian Marconi, est. 1922) was one of Canada's first radio stations.

The YMCA Quebec website describes Kanawana's contemporary experience as including 'sitting around a camp fire, singing call-and-response songs in the forest.' This confirms that campfire singing with call-and-response format remains a current tradition at the camp.

Color War (known as L&V Games at Kanawana) traditionally includes team cheers and songs as a central component at YMCA camps across North America. Teams present songs, cheers, and an 'Alma Mater' during a culminating event called 'Sing.' Songs are typically rewrites of popular tunes with team-specific lyrics. This provides the likely framework for L&V section cheers at Kanawana.

On May 16, 2023, a fire completely destroyed the superintendent's house (maison du surintendant) at Camp Kanawana. The building was located on Montée Sainte-Elmire in the Spring Valley sector, isolated from the campers' area. A passerby called firefighters at 6 AM. Twenty-five firefighters from Saint-Sauveur, Morin-Heights, and Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs responded. No injuries (camp was unoccupied). Cause undetermined. Total loss.
The Camp Kanawana infirmary has 5 beds and a private washroom. An emergency oxygen tank and AED are available.
Camp Kanawana has a 30-foot rock climbing wall among its current facilities.
Camp Kanawana has a separate pavilion for workshops and training sessions, listed as a distinct facility from other named pavilions.

The Kamp Kanawana Marching Song (also known as the Kanawana Cheer) includes a hushing call-and-response ('Shhhh'), followed by 'Kamp Kanawana, are you ready?! Then let's go!', the refrain 'Hail, hail, the gang's all here', spelling 'K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A, Kanawana!', and ends with 'It's true!'

The lost verses of the Kanawana Marching Song were rediscovered in the Kanawana Archives at Concordia University in 2006. The original song had three verses; only the first verse survived as part of the current cheer. The document containing the lost verses was undated. The original author of the Kanawana Marching Song is unknown.
The lost verses of the Kanawana Marching Song reference 'our camping songs' and include the line 'We're gonna tramp, tramp, tramp on through the rain.'

Matt Aronson created the Spirit of Kanawana blog (kanawana.blogspot.com) after a dinner with 'old kampers' where discussion turned to Kamp history and traditions. The blog is described as 'An open journal dedicated to the history, culture and traditions of Kamp Kanawana.' He signs posts with 'Non Nobis Solum, Matt.'
Matt Aronson has a theory that the Kanawana Marching Song arrived at Kamp via 'the tradition of Green Triangle.' He promised to elaborate in a future blog post, but no such post has been found.

Matthew E. Aronson is an attorney at Adessky Attorneys (Westmount), primarily an immigration lawyer. He is a City Councillor for District 7, Westmount. He lives in Westmount with wife Jenny and daughters Abby and Nell. He is a McGill University Faculty of Law graduate and member of the YMCA Kanawana Alumni Awards committee.
A Kanawana Flickr photo collection exists at flickr.com/photos/kanawana/ containing 4,416 photographs.

Around 1948-49, an 18-year-old William Shatner worked as a volunteer counsellor at Camp B'nai Brith in Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts (approximately 30 km from Kanawana in the Laurentians), where he earned respect by acting out ghost stories going bunk to bunk each night. He credits this experience with pushing him toward acting.

The Quebec Loup-Garou legend is distinctive: transformation results from religious transgression (missing Mass for 7 consecutive Sundays), not from being bitten. The Quebec Gazette reported a werewolf attack on July 21, 1766, at St. Rock near Cap Mouraska.

La Dame Blanche (White Lady of Montmorency Falls) is a Quebec ghost story about a bride whose fiance was killed at the Battle of Beauport (1759). La Corriveau (Marie-Josephe Corriveau, 1761) is one of Quebec's most enduring ghost stories.

Charles 'Smillie' Buckland attended Camp Kanawana from 1944 to 1951 and described being the 'first recipient of the coveted Green Triangle.' His memoir describes arriving by train from Montreal Central Station and bus up a gravel road to camp.

Camp Kanawana has 16 commercial Clivus Multrum composting units accommodating 22,500 uses each per year, and 32 dry toilets saving 576,000 gallons of water annually. Two central buildings contain all bathroom and shower facilities. The system eliminated the old septic system to keep Lake Kanawana safe from pollution.

The architectural firm Ross & Macdonald designed a 'Doctor's Cottage for Kamp Kanawana'. Architectural drawings are held in the Ross & Macdonald fonds at the Canadian Centre for Architecture (CCA). Ross & Macdonald also designed 'several buildings for the YMCA in Montréal (1909-13)', including the NDG YMCA Building.

Ross & Macdonald was a prominent Montreal architectural firm active from 1904 to 1942. Founded as Ross & MacFarlane in 1904 by George Allen Ross and David Huron MacFarlane. Robert Henry Macdonald replaced MacFarlane as partner in late 1912. The firm designed major Canadian landmarks including the Chateau Laurier, Royal York Hotel, Mount Royal Hotel, and Maple Leaf Gardens.

The McConnell Foundation provided $700,000 in funding (2023-2027) to the YMCAs of Quebec for major renovations at Camp Kanawana. The grant contributes to the YMCA Springboard for Life campaign and supports Kanawana as a '3-season outdoor and environmental education centre.'

The YMCA Springboard for Life (Tremplin pour la vie) campaign aimed to raise $20 million over five years. Campaign co-chairs were Gregory Chrispin (Desjardins), Sean Finn (CN), and Genevieve Marcon (GM Developpement). Desjardins contributed $1 million in May 2018, part of which was for a new community pavilion at Kanawana.
GLCRM Architectes Inc. and Garoy Construction Inc. are listed as major partners of the YMCAs of Quebec Foundation alongside Fondation Desjardins.
Concordia University Archives hold 'Layout, Building Designs, and Equipment' records dated 1946 for Kamp Kanawana in the YMCA of Montreal Fonds (P0145/12A, Committees sub-series).

The Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12B03 ('Land, facilities, equipment, supplies') contains records specific to Kanawana property and buildings. The sub-series also includes blueprints and maps among its materials.

In summer 2024, the YMCAs of Quebec launched 'Kanawana Adventure' (Aventure a Kanawana), a new day camp program for ages 5-12 on the Camp Kanawana site. The program is in English and focuses on nature immersion, wilderness survival, water sports, and arts. Marie-Pierre Lacasse is the Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana.

Camp Kanawana's property size is reported as 550 acres on the YMCA's official website. An older third-party source (Wikimapia) states 455 acres. The discrepancy may reflect additional land acquisition over time or a difference in measurement.
Camp Kanawana is described as a 'year-round environmental education facility and summer camp' in the Clivus Multrum project listing, confirming its use beyond the summer season.

Camp Kanawana has 'nature interpretation trails' across its 500+ acres of mature forest. The YMCA website describes the trails as opportunities to 'explore our hiking trails and head off to discover the marvels of our site.' No individual trail names are published.

Grace McMorris authored 'An Experience That Lasts a Lifetime: Building Modernity, Man, and Nation at the YMCA of Montreal's Kamp Kanawana, 1894-1967,' an MA thesis in History at Concordia University completed August 2023, supervised by Peter Gossage.

The YMCA facilities page lists the camp as having a 'boating waterfront with canoes, kayaks, paddleboards, a barge and a rescue boat' -- confirming the barge and rescue boat as distinct waterfront equipment.

Cabins at Camp Kanawana in the junior sections (Woodsmen and Pioneers) accommodate 10 people: 6 upper bunks, 4 lower bunks, with 2 staff members in their own small room within the cabin, and cubbies for each camper.

Platform tents at Camp Kanawana in the senior sections (Coureurs des Bois, Pathfinders, Rangers, Trailblazers, Voyageurs, Foresters and Adventurers) consist of a wooden platform with bunk beds covered by a heavy canvas tent and waterproof tarp, housing 8 campers and 1-2 staff members sharing the same space.

The Pathfinders and Pioneers groups at Camp Kanawana are made up of girls and non-binary campers; Coureurs des Bois and Woodsmen consist of boys and non-binary campers; Senior Kanawanians and Voyageurs are co-ed groups.
The Dining Hall at Camp Kanawana has an industrial kitchen that is not available to rental groups.
Camp Kanawana's address is 673 Montee Saint-Elmire, Saint-Sauveur, Quebec, Canada, J0R 1R1. The YMCA office is at 1440 Rue Stanley, Montreal H3A 1P7.

Camp Kanawana is available for rental year-round for groups of 6-250 persons, and in limited capacity during summer and winter for groups of 6-26 persons. The rental season runs from approximately May 21 to June 23 and August 20 to October 14.

There were two distinct individuals named Hedley Dimock connected to YMCA/camping: Hedley Seldon Dimock (1891-1958) the pioneering camp researcher, and Hedley G. Dimock (born c.1928) who conducted the Kanawana counselor research studies
Hedley Seldon Dimock (1891-1958) was born February 11, 1891 in South Rawdon, Hants, Nova Scotia
Hedley S. Dimock was a WWI veteran who served with Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry; in August 1918 he was severely wounded after throwing himself on a German grenade to protect his unit

Hedley S. Dimock and Charles E. Hendry conducted pioneering camp research at Camp Ahmek, Algonquin Park, Ontario, starting in 1923, published as 'Camping and Character: A Camp Experiment in Character Education' (Association Press, 1929/1931)
Hedley S. Dimock was dean of YMCA College in Chicago (later George Williams College) where in 1930 he launched institutes on the role of camps in 'character education' of children
The ACA's Hedley S. Dimock Award, established 1965, recognizes contributions to camping through related fields such as outdoor education, conservation, medicine, education, or social sciences
Hedley G. Dimock became first Chairman of the Department of Applied Social Science and Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies at Sir George Williams University in 1963
Hedley G. Dimock co-initiated a Community Development Study of the Cree of Mistassini-Chibougamau, Quebec in 1962
Hedley G. Dimock collaborated extensively with Dr. Raye Kass at Concordia University on group development publications; Kass was hired as Assistant Professor of Applied Human Sciences in 1972

R.L. Charlton, author of 'Notes re Early Days of YMCA Camps at Lake St. Joseph and Kanawana' (1943), was a Montreal independent marine surveyor, Treasurer of the Canadian Board of Marine Underwriters, and an 'ardent YMCA worker' who served with the YMCA in France during WWI supporting Canadian troops

Harold C. Cross authored 'One Hundred Years of Service to Youth' (also known as 'One Hundred Years: The Story of the Montreal YMCA'), a centennial history covering 1851-1951; manuscript, draft chapters, and printer quotations are in the Concordia archives (P0145/1B)

Harold Cross and Murray Ross corresponded while simultaneously writing their respective YMCA histories (Montreal Association and national Canadian YMCA) circa 1950; their correspondence survives in the Concordia fonds

Murray George Ross (1910-2000) served as founding President of York University (1959-1970) after a career as YMCA staff member; he authored 'The YMCA in Canada: The Chronicle of a Century' (Ryerson Press, 1951, 517 pages)

The Internet Archive 'ymca-montreal-fonds' collection, uploaded by Concordia University Records Management since September 2022, contains at least 25 digitized items including annual reports (1856, 1876, 1889-1890, 1891-1892, 1993), historical publications, photographs, and Kanawana-specific materials
Alfred Sandham published 'History of the Montreal YMCA' in 1873, the earliest known history of the Montreal YMCA; digitized on Internet Archive

On July 7, 1913, The Montreal Gazette reported two detachments of Montreal YMCA boys leaving for Kamp Kanawana, with programme adapted for specific ages including instruction in athletics, educational subjects, and Bible study; speakers included M.F. Furey (physical director) and Dr. Hamilton

In July 1918, Kamp Kanawana was visited by Mr. and Mrs. Frank Lawes of London, England, who were touring the world filming YMCA work; a reel of camp activities was added to their collection, making it potentially the earliest known film footage of Kanawana
Stuart McLean recorded 'A Letter from Camp' for the Vinyl Cafe 'Up & Away' 4-CD collection (2016, Disc Three), in which he 'inserts a personal story from his own days at his beloved summer camp'

Complete Pip Award recipients: 2007 Richard 'Itche' Kerr, 2008 Rick Patten, 2009 Stuart McLean, 2011 Bruce Netherwood, 2012 John Cleghorn, 2013 Sam Lazarus (posthumous) & Lazarus family, 2014 Jeniene Phillips Birks, 2015 Terry 'Aislin' Mosher, 2016 Carol Skinner, 2017 Chris Adam, 2018 Marina Sharpe (no 2010 recipient listed)

Samuel Karl Lazarus (born March 3, 1978) died January 14, 2004 in Kumasi, Ghana, of cerebral malaria at age 25; the Samuel Lazarus Fund was established at Kamp Kanawana, 1435 Drummond Street, 4th Floor, Montreal

The A. Ross Seaman Memorial Fund was established in 1987 at Concordia University to honour his dedication to Concordia, Dawson College, Kamp Kanawana, and the YMCA; provides annual awards for leadership and scholarship

The Kamp Kanawana Marching Song refrain 'Hail, hail, the gang's all here' derives from the 1915 American song 'Alabama Jubilee' by D.A. Esrom (pseudonym of Dolly Morse), set to a tune from Arthur Sullivan's 'The Pirates of Penzance'; lost verses were rediscovered in the Kanawana Archives at Concordia in 2006

The Canadian Centre for Architecture holds architectural drawings for a Doctor's Cottage at Kamp Kanawana by Ross & Macdonald, one of Canada's most prominent architectural firms (designers of Mount Royal Hotel, Chateau Laurier, Union Station Toronto)

Lac Kanawana has a surface area of 0.235 km2, maximum depth 12.5m, mean depth 5.4m, altitude 318.4m, watershed 5.17 km2, and water renewal time of 0.43 years; located in Saint-Sauveur, MRC Les Pays-d'en-Haut
The municipality changed its name from Howard Township to Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard in 1939; Villa Howard earned the reputation 'Miami of the Laurentians' in the 1950s
Emma Anders recorded 'Feels Like Home (Live)' inspired by 'the magic of Coyote Camp at YMCA Kanawana August 21st-25th, 2017', confirming 'Coyote Camp' as a program name at Kanawana
The McMorris thesis author is Grace McMorris (not 'Tina' as previously recorded in some project notes); completed August 22, 2023, convocation Fall 2023; advisor was Peter Gossage; eprint ID 992763
Concordia's Records Management and Archives (RMA) reached a milestone of 5,000 items uploaded to Internet Archive as of December 2022; the YMCA fonds digitization began uploading in September 2022
Camp YMCA Kanawana maintains active social media: Instagram @ymcakanawana (1,824 followers, 571 posts), TikTok @campymcakanawana, and X/Twitter @YMCA_Kanawana
Frank Crabbe was an ex-Weredale Boy who died in the Vietnam War in 1966, connecting the YMCA Montreal camp community (Camp Lewis, Weredale House) to the broader social history of the 1960s

The 1993 promotional film 'Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that Lasts a Lifetime' was directed by Cathy Reeves, produced by Laurentien Productions for the Montreal YMCA; 9-minute VHS with voiceover narration and camper testimonials; an access copy is reportedly on YouTube per the Concordia catalog

The Concordia archives (P0145/12N03) contain records of the Canadian Camping Association founding (1936-1937), constitution (1937, 1942), executive meetings (1937-1942), camping school at McGill University (1937-1940), and lists of camps/officials/counsellors (1939-1948)
Leigh Evans attended Camp Kanawana for 6 summers: 1 as a camper, 1 as a Leader-in-Training, and 4 as staff. She was named Capitaine for the Voyageur team of the L&V Games in 2012.

Leigh Evans described Camp Kanawana's 'Party Barge' — a large raft decorated for celebrations, used for a surprise birthday party for a 12-year-old camper. She credited Kanawana with shaping her career as an educator.
Leigh Evans wrote of Camp Kanawana: 'If you've never been, you can't understand it and if you have been, you can't explain it.'

The Concordia Archives Communications sub-sub-series (P0145/12B04) includes camp brochures (1921-1990s), radio broadcast scripts (1936-1941), Kanawana Outing Club posters, Knights of Kanawana artwork (1981), and a Kellogg's Frosted Flakes YMCA Camp Experience contest cereal box (1997)

CFCF, the station that broadcast the 1941 Kanawana promotional segment, was Canada's first radio station ('Canada's First, Canada's Finest'), established in 1919 from the Marconi Wireless experimental station XWA
On September 5, 2014, Camp YMCA Kanawana alumni assembled at Victoria Hall, Westmount to celebrate the camp's 120th anniversary reunion

Jonathan Birks serves as chair of Foundation Giving for the YMCA Kanawana Development Project, connecting the Birks family to camp philanthropy alongside the Pip Award connection through Jeniene Phillips Birks (2014 recipient)
A. Ross Seaman was Director of Kamp Kanawana for many years and earlier had a career in community work and the camping movement with the YMCA

A. Ross Seaman served as teacher and chairperson of the Community Recreation and Leadership Training (CRLT) Department at Dawson College from 1974 to 1984, where he helped establish a program focusing on camping, leadership, and community organization

In 1963, A. Ross Seaman was a part-time faculty member in Applied Social Science at Sir George Williams University, concurrent with Hedley G. Dimock's founding of the department; he was an active collaborator in the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies

After retiring from Dawson College, Seaman served as acting chair of Concordia University Leisure Studies during the 1986-87 school year; he and his wife Margaret were instrumental in developing the Elder Hostel Program at the Loyola Campus

A. Ross Seaman died in 1987. Five organizations give scholarships in his memory: Dawson College, Concordia University, Kamp Kanawana, the YMCA, and Vankleek Hill Collegiate (his home community in Ontario). The Dawson/CRLT scholarship is $500 for a second-year student.

Frank Edward Crabbe (born 1946, died February 16, 1966), ex-Weredale Boy and Camp Lewis counsellor c.1964-65, enlisted in the US Marine Corps January 7, 1965 in Albany, NY; assigned to Lima Co, 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines. Killed in action south of Hill 190, Ho Vang District, Quang Nam Province. Died of extreme burns at NSA Navy Hospital, Da Nang. Buried at Cimetière Notre-Dame-des-Neiges, Montreal

Weredale House, located below St. Catherine Street off Atwater in Montreal, was a four-story brick building built in the 1930s by the Rotary Club (who raised $289,000). It closed in 1977 and became part of Youth Horizons, formed from Allancroft Centre, Summerhill Homes, Weredale House, and Mount Bruno Girls Cottage School
In 1934, the Rotary Club of Westmount purchased 260 acres with a mile of shoreline on Lac l'Achigan, 55 miles north of Montreal, for Camp Weredale — the summer camp for Weredale House boys

Hedley G. Dimock retired from Concordia University in 1980; Richard D. McDonald, who joined in 1965, succeeded him as Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies. In November 1997, Applied Social Science amalgamated with Leisure Studies to form the Department of Applied Human Sciences

After retirement, Hedley G. Dimock became Director of the Centre for Human Resource Development (independent consulting/research organization) in Puslinch, Ontario; adjunct professor at University of Guelph; served on faculties of 8 universities including McGill, Columbia, Toronto, and Concordia; worked with over 300 organizations across Canada; five of his books published in Japanese

Hedley G. Dimock's publications include: 'How to Observe Your Group', 'How to Analyze and Evaluate Group Growth', 'Planning Group Development', 'Factors in Working with Groups', 'The Child in Hospital', 'Planning Staff Training Programs', 'Training for Planned Change', 'Groups', 'Designing and Facilitating Training Programs', 'Simplified Guide to Program Evaluation', 'Intervention and Empowerment', 'Administration of the Modern Camp'. Co-authored with Raye Kass: 'Leading and Managing Dynamic Groups' (Captus Press, 2008), 'How to Observe Your Group' (4th ed, 2007)

Hedley Seldon Dimock (1891-1958) was married to Elizabeth Marguerite Gardiner and had 2 children; parents were Charles Turner Torry Dimock and Catherine E. Dimock. He was Director of Training for the United Service Organization (USO) during WWII

The SGW/Concordia Department of Applied Social Science grew directly from Sir George Williams University's roots in the YMCA of Montreal; in the 1940s, YMCA/SGW offered courses in counselling, group work, organization development, and supervision as part of a B.A. Principal Robert C. Rae co-envisioned the formal department with Hedley G. Dimock in 1963

In 1926, Msgr. McShane founded Camp Kinkora on 3 km² of private land near Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard for English Catholic children. Philanthropist Charles Pripstein also built a camp for Jewish children in the area. The creation of Camp Otoreke 'marked the beginning of a wave of tourism for Saint-Adolphe that never dried up'

Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard is approximately 11 km from the train station in Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts, which historically deterred winter (ski) tourism. Vacationers came from Quebec, Canada, the United States, and even South America

Hedley Gardner Dimock's full name is Hedley Gardner Dimock (not just 'Hedley G. Dimock'). His middle name 'Gardner' closely resembles the maiden name of H.S. Dimock's wife, Elizabeth Marguerite Gardiner, providing strong circumstantial evidence for a father-son relationship.
Hedley Gardner Dimock's education: BA from Beloit College; MA and EdD from Columbia University.
Hedley Seldon Dimock died October 4, 1958 in Burlingame, San Mateo, California. Obituary published in Oakland Tribune, October 5, 1958.

Hedley Seldon Dimock enlisted with the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry (PPCLI) via the University of Saskatchewan group in Saskatoon in 1917. In August 1918, he threw himself on a German grenade to protect his unit and was severely wounded. It was months after the war before he could return to Canada and resume his studies.
During the Second World War, Hedley Seldon Dimock served as Director of Training for the United Service Organization (USO).

Camping and Character (1929/1931) was published by Association Press, New York, with a foreword by William H. Kilpatrick (progressive educator and colleague of John Dewey at Columbia). The book is 364 pages, illustrated, divided into two parts: Part 1 on camp experience and character-building potential, Part 2 a case study of character education at Camp Ahmek.

At the time of the 1923 Camp Ahmek study, both Dimock and Hendry were affiliated with Columbia University, New York. Charles E. Hendry later served at the University of Toronto School of Social Work, retiring in 1969.
Hedley S. Dimock co-authored Talks to Counselors (1939) with Taylor Statten, founder of Camp Ahmek. This was a direct collaboration between the two camp education pioneers.

The first recipients of the ACA Hedley S. Dimock Award (1965) were Julian W. Smith (director, Outdoor Education Project, Michigan State University), Sigurd F. Olson (author and environmentalist), and Stewart L. Udall (U.S. Secretary of the Interior under JFK and LBJ).

George Williams College in Chicago was originally founded in 1884 as the Western Secretarial Institute of the YMCA on the shores of Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. It was renamed George Williams College in 1933. The college was 'frequently referred to as the group work school.' Dimock, Hendry, Everett Du Vall, and Harleigh B. Trecker were key faculty.

A third Hedley Dimock — Hedley Gilbert Dimock, Pilot Officer (Flight Engineer), RCAF, service number C/92344 — died June 27, 1944 in a take-off accident in India. He is buried at Madras War Cemetery. His father was Charles Albert Dimock, a different family line from H.S. Dimock's father Charles Turner Torry Dimock.

Raye Kass (born Rachel R. Kass, 1938) attended Sir George Williams University in 1970 (BA with Distinction), earned MSW at University of Toronto (1972), was hired as Assistant Professor at Concordia 1972, promoted to Associate Professor 1976, Professor 2012. She served as past Program Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies (CHRCS) and has conducted over 1,000 workshops. Involved in space research with Canadian Space Agency, NASA, and Russian Space Agency.

The Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies at SGW was 'a research, consultation and training service of the Department' of Applied Social Science, created 1963 under the vision of Principal Robert C. Rae and Dr. Hedley G. Dimock. Both grew 'directly out of Sir George Williams University's roots in the community, specifically through the YMCA of Montreal.'

Hedley G. Dimock published 'Improving Communication Skills through Training' in the Journal of Communication, Vol. 11, Issue 3 (1961) — his earliest known publication. He also published Group Development (1966, Sir George Williams University edition) and the first edition of How to Observe Your Group (1970, solo author).

Hedley S. Dimock authored Rediscovering the Adolescent: A Study of Personality Development in Adolescent Boys (1937, Association Press), co-authored The Supervision of Group Work and Recreation with Harleigh Bradley Trecker, co-authored A Professional Outlook on Group Education (1938) with Karl P. Zerfess and Charles E. Hendry, and authored Designing Education in Values (1955) with Roy Sorenson.

The Dimock-Kass publications include the 'Dimock Series on Groups' published by Captus Press: Leading and Managing Dynamic Groups (4th ed., 2008), How to Observe Your Group (4th ed., 2007), Comment observer votre groupe (French ed., 2010), Making Work Groups Effective (6th ed., 2011). Earlier editions of some titles were co-authored with Irene Devine before Kass joined.

In 1962, the Community Development Study of the Cree of the Mistassini-Chibougamau Region of Quebec was co-initiated by Hedley G. Dimock and Richard D. McDonald. A related publication, 'The Impact of Culture Change on Mistassini Cree Youth,' appeared in the Canadian Psychiatric Association Journal, Vol. 19, No. 4 (1974).
Lac St. Joseph (Camp Jubilee site) was a 33-acre property purchased in 1898 at a cost of one dollar per acre.
The early Camp Jubilee had half a dozen sleeping tents, a dining marquee, and a small fleet of primitive boats.
53 members used the Camp Jubilee site at Lac St. Joseph in its first summer (1894).
210 campers attended Camp Jubilee in 1903.
The name 'Kanawana' was adopted around 1910 when the camp moved to the Saint-Sauveur site. Camp Jubilee at Lake St. Joseph was never called Kanawana.

Harold C. Cross's book was published as: Harold C. Cross, One Hundred Years of Service with Youth: The Story of the Montreal Y.M.C.A (Montreal: Association Press, 1951). Association Press was the YMCA's own publishing imprint.
Harold C. Cross introduced the 'Kickers and Knockers' council system at Kanawana in 1925.
W.J.G. MacDiarmid (McMorris archival form) is the same person as Greig Macdiarmid (1935 History, Green Triangle). 'Greig' maps to the 'G' initial.
A. Ross Seaman served as director of Kamp Kanawana from 1959 to 1967. He oversaw the 1959 section renaming and the La Vérendrye expansion.
The name 'Kanawana' does not exist in Kanien'kéha (the Mohawk language). The closest attested Kanien'kéha term is 'kanà:wa' meaning 'swamp'. McMorris notes the phonetic similarity to Kahnawá:ke.
The motto 'Each for all and all for each' is documented in a 1927 source (in addition to 1922 brochure). The Latin motto 'Non Nobis Solum' is first attested in the 1993 YMCA video.
'Dear Old Kanawana' was the camp song before the Richard Kerr composition, sung to the tune of the Battle Hymn of the Republic. Referenced in the Council of Tribes ceremony script (c. 1925-1927).

'My Kanawana' poem/song used as epigraph for Chapter 1 of McMorris thesis. Full text: 'My Kanawana, My Kanawana, / Where the trees and wild flowers grow, / Where the rippling waters flow, / Where the golden sunbeams glow, / My Kanawana, My Kanawana, / I will never let you go.'

By 1945, canoe trip routes were codified into a tiered system: 3-day Lachute trip for beginners, 7-8 day trips to Île Perrot and Grenville for intermediates, and a 10-day Ottawa River trip for seniors.
The La Vérendrye canoe trip program was formally named 'Les Voyageurs de La Vérendrye.' The YMCA secured a 25-acre lease at Lac Landron as a base camp.
In 1959, eighteen canoe trips went out from the Pathfinder section alone during the first season at La Vérendrye.
By 1964, over twenty canoe trips were departing each season from La Vérendrye.

In the L&V Games (by 1958), the Voyageur team leader was called the 'Capitaine' and the Lumberman team leader was called the 'Boss'. The opening ceremony on Sunday featured a floating bonfire on the lake.
The 1959 section renaming replaced all four sections: Bantams became Pioneers, Juveniles became Woodsmen, Juniors became Coureurs de Bois, Seniors became Pathfinders.
The 1941 scarlet fever outbreak at Kanawana required a full month of quarantine.
The 1944 mumps outbreak at Kanawana occurred during weeks six and seven of the season.

In the 1946 polio outbreak at Kanawana (6 cases), Dr. Cushing (a pediatrician) visited the camp and recommended cancelling trips but keeping camp open. Three of six cases were discharged by end of summer.
During WWII, Kanawana hosted campers from England, France, Scotland, and Poland — not only British evacuees.
The Pagé farm was purchased in 1960 as an expansion of the Kanawana camp property.
1910 was the first season at the Saint-Sauveur site, confirmed by McMorris and consistent with the 1935 History's 'twenty-sixth year of existence'.
The first girls admitted to Kanawana were aged 10 to 12, entering the youngest section of the camp.

The Council of Tribes ceremony (c. 1925-1927) featured a Big Chief presiding over four Little Chiefs: Chief Winnemucca (Ojibways), Chief Tshut-che-nau (Tuscaroras), Chief Teuskewata (Algonquins), and Chief Watotopa (Cayugas). Named braves challenged each other to physical competitions including Indian leg wrestling, neck pulling, and crab walking.

The Council of Tribes ceremony concluded with the Big Chief calling on the assembly to 'sing the song of the tribes of Kanawana' (Dear Old Kanawana, to the Battle Hymn of the Republic), followed by a closing invocation and chant: 'Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe.'

A typical Indian Council Ring program (described by the 1939 juvenile section director) included: a torch parade to the council ring, a peace pipe ceremony, Indian dances around the fire, and a story on 'moral nature, generally pertaining to the North American Indian.'

The 'Zuni Council' script (1931) was a multi-part drama featuring settler-Indigenous conflict culminating in a Jesuit priest healing sick braves and persuading the Chief to surrender his lands to settlers.

The CCA Centenary Journey Kanawana section ran from Deep River, Ontario to Britannia Beach (west Ottawa), August 2-9, 1967. Trip report by Yves St. Pierre covered Ottawa River route history from archaeological prehistory through Champlain's 1613 exploration.

Participants in the 1967 CCA Centenary Journey wore colourful plaid 'lumberman' shirts and decorated their canoes with decals and crests. Upon arrival at Britannia Beach, a busload of Kanawana campers greeted them singing the camp song.
The Ottawa Journal covered the arrival of the Kanawana CCA Centenary Journey paddlers on August 10, 1967. McMorris thesis Figure 3.5 shows the campers arriving.
McMorris thesis examining committee: Dr. Elena Razlogova (chair), Dr. Gavin Taylor, Dr. Theresa Ventura. Supervisor: Dr. Peter Gossage.
Nelson McEwen served as camp director in 1930-1931.
R.H. Hanagan served as camp director in 1942 and 1946, writing detailed season reports. He managed the 1946 polio outbreak.

Deep River, Ontario was chosen as the starting point for the Quebec section of the CCA Centenary Journey because it was historically the oldest and most well-established site of voyageur ritual baptism on the fur trade route.
The Kanawana camp director's wife was present at camp in 1930, described as a 'refining influence.'
During the first summer at the Saint-Sauveur site in 1910, sixty-six members attended camp between June 19 and July 17.

Lyrics of 'Dear Old Kanawana' (to Battle Hymn of the Republic): 'Mine eyes have seen the glories of a thousand camps or more / By placid inland waters and the ocean's mighty roar / But now I've seen old Kanawana, I'll never wander more / I'll ever camp right here. // Glory, glory, Kanawana / Dear old, good old Kanawana / We the boys of Kanawana / Will ever camp right here.'

Lyrics of 'My Kanawana': 'My Kanawana, Kamp of the free / Spirit mind and body unite to proclaim democracy / Our Kanawana - your Kamp and mine / Lake and Hill and Sky unite to proclaim God's soul divine / Wind thru' the pines - sunsets aglow - pals on the trail as on and up we go / Our Kanawana - Kamp of the free / Spirit body mind unite to proclaim democracy.'
In 1942, Kanawana 'welcomed the Boys of Tamaracouta' with a programme that featured fire-lighting, hymns, and prayers (Fire of Friendship ceremony).
Campers travelling to Lac St. Joseph took the train to Sainte-Agathe, then a two-hour drive by horse and springless buckboard to the camp site.
Of 66 members attending Kanawana in 1910, 31 boys 'decided for the Christian life.'
In 1912, Kanawana served boys from four YMCA branches: Westmount, Point St. Charles, North, and Central.
In 1918, Kanawana cost $8.00 per week.
In 1922, there were 391 campers at Kanawana, including 16 'unattached' (non-YMCA members).
In 1929, Kanawana campers came from Quebec City, Toronto, New Brunswick, and Havana, Cuba.
By the 1930s, Kanawana opened to non-YMCA members.
In 1930, 10-year-olds were allowed at Kanawana and the Juvenile section (ages 10-12) was created.
In the early 1940s, 8-year-olds were allowed at Kanawana and the Bantam section was created.
Camp Tamaracouta (Boy Scouts) was established southeast of Kanawana in 1912.
YWCA Camp Oolahwan was located near Sainte-Marguerite de Lac Masson and operated from 1917 to 2005.
In 1936, MacDiarmid recorded weight statistics: 85 campers neither gained nor lost, 195 gained a total of 585 lbs, 30 lost a total of 54 lbs (net gain 531 lbs).
In 1942, a 'full-blooded Iroquois' spent 3 days at Kanawana teaching woodcraft.
In 1946, Kanawana campers were covered in cocoa powder to greet visitors from Camp Oolahwan as 'Indians.'
In 1936, 'minstrel shows' were mentioned in the Kanawana juvenile section schedule.

A 1928 Kanawana map showed 4 Indian characters and over 20 white boy characters. By 1962, the map removed Indian characters but retained labels for Indian Grave, Council Ring, and Indians and Settlers.
By 1962, cottager community growth near Kanawana meant driving canoe trips over 150 km away.
In 1959, the Pathfinder section went on 18 canoe trips to the Rouge River, North River, Lake Kiamika, and Taureau.
In 1946, a camper named Rosenthal was found 'guilty of disobedience and thoughtlessness' and sentenced to 2 days fatigue duty at 'the Ritz' (camp toilets).
The Concordia YMCA fonds contains approximately 125 metres of textual records.
entities: Concordia University Records Management and Archives

facts.claim: The Canadian Centre for Architecture (CCA) holds architectural drawings by Ross & Macdonald for a Doctor's Cottage at Kamp Kanawana, in the Ross & Macdonald fonds.

Ross & Macdonald was one of Canada's most prominent early 20th-century architectural firms, based in Montreal, responsible for the Royal York Hotel in Toronto, T. Eaton Company stores, Union Station Toronto, and Central Station Ottawa.

A documentary titled 'Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that Lasts a Lifetime' was directed by Cathy Reeves in 1993, featuring voiceover narration and camper testimonials. It is held in the Concordia University archives (YMCA of Montreal fonds).
entities: Concordia University Records Management and Archives

facts.claim: A radio broadcast about YMCA Kamp Kanawana aired on Station CFCF on June 26, 1941. A recording is held on the Internet Archive, uploaded by Concordia University Records Management.

Stuart McLean (April 19, 1948 - February 15, 2017), host of CBC Radio's The Vinyl Cafe, worked as a counsellor at Camp Kanawana for five summers starting in 1969, and served as assistant camp director in 1974 and 1975.

Stuart McLean credited Camp Kanawana with transforming his life, calling it 'the first place, as a young person, that I felt I could contribute to the greater good.' Before becoming a counsellor in 1969, he described himself as 'an utter academic, athletic and social failure' who had to repeat Grade 11.
After Stuart McLean's death, his family established the Stuart McLean Camp YMCA Kanawana Fund to help children and teens without financial means attend Camp Kanawana.
entities: Stuart McLean Camp YMCA Kanawana Fund

facts.claim: A Flickr account named 'Kanawana' hosts 4,416 photographs related to Camp Kanawana.
Camp YMCA Kanawana's 120th anniversary reunion was held on September 5, 2014, at Victoria Hall, with alumni (former campers and staff) assembling to celebrate.

The Pip Award is given annually to a former camper, counsellor, or supervisor at Camp YMCA Kanawana who best exemplifies the values of selflessness and contribution to the community. The Pip Award Committee is composed of Kanawana alumni.
Camp Kanawana is listed in the Canadian Geographical Names Database (Natural Resources Canada) under ID EKWXQ, confirming its official place-name status.
Camp Kanawana's official motto is 'Non Nobis Solum' (Latin: 'Not for ourselves alone' / French: 'Pas seulement pour nous-memes').
Camp Kanawana's current tuck shop sells camp-related swag items. Every camper receives a water bottle on their first day and a camp t-shirt and group/camp photos upon departure.
In 1942, Camp Director R.H. Hanagan and Resident Director E.E. Smee organized a circus and parade at Kamp Kanawana, with Hanagan appearing in Indian garb on horseback
The 1942 Kanawana circus featured booths and tents with games including darts, nail and hammer contests, hoop-la, and cocoanut shy, organized for Bantam, Junior, Intermediate, and Senior sections
In February 1933, The Gazette reported on 'Music and Comedy in Fossils' Revue' associated with Kanawana, suggesting an alumni/reunion group called the 'Fossils'
Camp Kanawana closed for the 2020 and 2021 summers due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions on overnight camps in Quebec
Camp Kanawana usually has about 900 campers every year (as of 2021)
Kate Taylor was Camp Kanawana director during the 2021 COVID closure decision
Stuart McLean first visited Kanawana in summer 1969, was hired as counsellor in the senior boys section that same summer, and served as assistant camp director in 1974 and 1975
In 2022, Camp Kanawana introduced a co-ed 'gender-expansive' tent option for the first time, in addition to separate boys and girls accommodations

Camp Weredale was founded in 1934 by the Rotary Club of Westmount, which bought 260 acres with a mile of shoreline on Lac l'Achigan, 55 miles north of Montreal, and gave the property to Weredale House.
Camp Weredale was established as a summer home for orphaned or at-risk boys living at Weredale House (originally the Boys' Home of Montreal, founded 1870 by Charles Alexander).
Camp Weredale is located at 1300 chemin Weredale, Saint-Hippolyte, Quebec, on Lac l'Achigan in the Laurentians.

Concordia University Archives hold YMCA of Montreal records related to Camp Weredale dated 1977-1983, including a proposed two-site operation involving Kanawana and Weredale, and situation reports profiling Kamp Kanawana, Camp Otoreke, and Camp Weredale.
In 1977, the YMCA of Montreal proposed a two-site operation involving Kanawana and Weredale.
Camp Weredale suffered a fire and was reconstructed in 1965.
In 1977, Weredale House joined with Summerhill Homes, the Girls' Cottage School, and Allencroft Reception Centres to form Youth Horizons (now part of Batshaw Youth and Family Centres).
Camp Ouareau was founded in 1922 by two school teachers, Mabel Jamieson and Ferna Halliday, as one of the earliest summer camps exclusively for girls in Canada.
Camp Ouareau co-founder Mabel Jamieson was National Student Secretary of the Christian Association of Young Women of Canada in 1915, and was secretary general of the YMCA of Montreal.

Camp Ouareau is located at Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci, on Lac Ouareau in the Lanaudiere region, about 1.5 hours north of Montreal. The name 'Ouareau' is of Algonquin origin meaning 'far away' or 'distant'.
The YWCA's Camp Oolahwan was founded in 1917 and held its centennial reunion at Camp Ouareau in St-Donat, Quebec, in August 2017.
Camp Otoreke (meaning 'home in the north') was the renamed Camp Jubilee. The YMCA changed the name in 1909. It operated until 1982 on the original Lake St. Joseph site in Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard.
In 1892, Lemuel Cushing of the Montreal YMCA brought a group of boys to Lake Saint-Joseph in Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, inaugurating the YMCA summer camping program.
Camp Jubilee was named after the fiftieth anniversary of the YMCA and was located on several islands in Lake Saint-Joseph with a landing area on shore.

Concordia Archives hold Camp Jubilee records including: fishing rights on Lake St. Joseph (1893-1902), a promotional letter (1895), land purchase correspondence (1897-1901), photographs (1898), and brochures (1898-1900).
YMCA Camp Pine Crest was founded in 1910 in Torrance, Ontario (Muskoka), and is now part of the YMCA of Greater Toronto. It is one of Canada's earliest overnight camps.
YMCA John Island Camp was established in 1954 on an island in the North Channel of Lake Huron, south of Spanish, Ontario. It is the overnight camp of the YMCA of Northeastern Ontario.
Big Cove YMCA Camp in Merigomish, Nova Scotia, founded in 1889, is the oldest residential camp in Canada. Camp Kanawana (1894) is the oldest in Quebec and the second oldest in Canada.

The Canadian Camping Association (CCA) was founded in 1936. The first meeting was held on May 20, 1936 at the Central YMCA, Toronto. Taylor Statten was first president; Mary Edgar was first vice-president.
The Ontario Camping Association archives at Trent University include a file for Camp Kanawana dated 1940.

Stuart McLean worked as a counsellor at Camp Kanawana beginning in 1969, serving five summers in the late 1960s and early 1970s, starting in the senior boys' section and eventually becoming assistant summer camp director.

Stuart McLean said of Camp Kanawana: 'I began pulling my adult self together at Camp Kanawana, and I benefited greatly from my camp experiences' and called it 'the first place I ever felt I truly belonged.'

After Stuart McLean's death in February 2017, his family established the Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund, requesting donations in lieu of flowers to help children without financial means attend Camp YMCA Kanawana.

Stuart McLean attended Sir George Williams University (now Concordia University). He once passed up a chance to study journalism at Carleton University to return to Camp Kanawana as assistant director.

A 1993 documentary 'Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that lasts a lifetime' (9 min) was produced by Laurentien Productions for the Montreal YMCA, directed by Cathy Reeves. It describes Kanawana as the oldest camp in Quebec and second oldest in Canada.
The YMCA of Quebec ran day camps at Concordia University (Fine Arts Camp, Science and Engineering Camp) alongside Camp Kanawana programs, until discontinuing day camps in fall 2025.
Camp Kanawana's motto is 'Non Nobis Solum' — 'Not for ourselves alone.'
Dave Twynam served as camp director of Kamp Kanawana. Correspondence from 'Camp director Dave Twynam' is dated 1979 in the Concordia YMCA archives (sub-sub-series P0145/12B01).

Ross Bannerman authored a 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' in 1969, listed in Concordia YMCA archives (sub-sub-series P0145/12B01). Role at camp not confirmed but authoring a camp report suggests administrative authority.

Concordia archives contain 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch Director's Report' for 1972 (5 copies) and 1970, plus 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' from 1974.

David Leduc managed YMCA Camp Kanawana's summer and winter programs per his LinkedIn (profile: davidgleduc), including recruitment/supervision of 75 employees, all programs and operational budgets, safety/security of 800 participants, reporting to Board of Directors, strategic business planning, and development/implementation of an intensive youth leadership program. Exact dates of tenure not specified but must predate his Oxfam-Quebec Lebanon role (Mar 2000-Jun 2002), placing Kanawana service likely in the late 1990s. Education: BA International Development (Dalhousie), MBA (McGill, 2006-2011). Subsequent career: Oxfam-Quebec Lebanon coordinator (2000-2002), McGill ICAN director of operations (~11 years), Executive Director of Development and Peace (2015-~2020), Director of Philanthropy Quebec at Pathways to Education Canada (current). Based in Greater Montreal (Outremont). Languages: English, French, Spanish, functional Arabic.

The anonymous Westmount Magazine commenter who was camp director at Kanawana in 1974-1975 (alongside Stuart McLean as assistant director) also sublet McLean's flat on Dorchester and looked after his piano when McLean moved to Toronto in the late 1970s. The commenter's name is not visible in available web results.

Concordia archives P0145/12B01 contains 'YMCA Kamp Kanawana Facts-timeline 1894-1998' and 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948), by Ben T. Hannah (1989)'. These documents likely contain comprehensive director lists.
'Kanawana, a Place to Grow: A Proposal for the Future of Kanawana, by Kanawana Camping Task Force' report from 1988 is held in Concordia archives P0145/12B01.

Sean Day is described as 'former director of Camp YMCA Kanawana' in recent references (post-2022), indicating he has left the director role. Kate Taylor and Kevin Slezak (Assistant Director) are current leadership.
On September 5, 2014, Camp YMCA Kanawana alumni assembled at Victoria Hall to celebrate the camp's 120th anniversary reunion.
A 1993 documentary about Camp Kanawana was produced, describing it as the oldest camp in Quebec and second oldest in Canada. This was one year before the 1994 centennial.
The Green Triangle camp newsletter dates from 1932-1940 per Concordia finding aid; additional issues (KA-News and Green Triangle) from 1976 and 1978-1982 are also held.
Standardized YMCA Camp Songs Books existed by 1938 (per eBay listing of lot of 7 books from that year), contemporaneous with Kanawana's song books (1941-1945) in the Concordia archives.
The YMCA published a formal Association Hymn Book in 1904, containing sacred hymns for male chorus, unaccompanied, in English. This is the only YMCA collection on IMSLP.
The YMCA published a Service Song Book during WWI, prepared by the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations, for men in military and naval service.

Camp Sloane YMCA organizes village cheers and chants by section/age group (Pioneer Girls, Junior Girls, Senior Girls, Student Girls, LEAD, CIT, Day Camp), confirming the YMCA tradition of section-specific cheers.

The L&V Games at Kanawana are 3 days long (not 2 as at Pine Crest). A former staff member described them as involving 'incredible teamwork, determination, and passion' where 'every person, campers and staff alike, unite with their team.'
Stuart McLean described Camp Kanawana as 'a microcosm of Canada, where English, French, rich, poor, recent immigrants and locals sing together around the camp fire.'

Stuart McLean described himself before camp as 'an utter academic, athletic and social failure' who 'didn't have a lot of confidence.' At camp he found 'a place where I was accepted by others and I was able to contribute to the greater good.'

The Camp Kanawana current sections include: Pioneers (girls/non-binary 7-12), Woodsmen (boys/non-binary 7-12), Coureurs des Bois (boys/non-binary 13-16), Pathfinders (girls/non-binary 13-16), Rangers (15-16 leadership), Voyageurs Ultimate (15-17 canoe-tripping leadership), Trailblazers, Foresters, Adventurers, Explorers, Senior Kanawanians, and Mountaineer (all-gender tent for transgender, non-binary, and gender non-conforming campers).
The Mountaineer program was launched at Kanawana as an all-gender tent to provide a safe and welcoming environment for transgender, non-binary, and gender non-conforming campers.

YMCA Camp Waabanaki (previously Camp Wabanaki) changed its name in early 2023 at the recommendation of a local elder as part of reconciliation with the local Indigenous community. The new name means 'a new dawn day.'

Taylor Statten established Camp Ahmek in 1921 at Canoe Lake in Algonquin Park. Statten's camp philosophy was a result of his 1905 role as Boys' Work Secretary for the Toronto YMCA and his role organizing a YMCA summer camp near Orillia.

The Canadian Summer Camp Research Project (CSCRP, 2006-2011) by the CCA and University of Waterloo interviewed over 50 camp directors and identified five common areas of youth development at camps: social connections/integration, environmental awareness, attitudes toward physical activity, emotional intelligence, and personal development/self-confidence.

Over 30 web searches for 'Chopsy' (also 'Chopsey', 'Chopsie') combined with camp, ghost, Quebec, Kanawana, and legend returned zero relevant results. The name does not appear in any indexed folklore archive, academic database, Reddit discussion, blog, or camp ghost story collection as of March 2026.

No web source connects any 'Richard Kerr' to YMCA camp song composition. The prominent Richard Kerr (songwriter, 1944-2023) was an English pop songwriter (co-wrote 'Mandy' for Barry Manilow) with no documented connection to camps or YMCAs. Richard 'Itch/Itche' Kerr, the Kanawana alumnus who composed 'On My Way to Kanawana' and received the inaugural Pip Award c. 2007, has no web presence.

No web source documents any Kanawana-specific lyrics, sheet music, or digital recording of 'On My Way to Kanawana.' The Concordia Archives CD (P145/SR0001) remains the sole known copy as of March 2026.

The Concordia YMCA of Montreal fonds finding aid page confirms holdings include: Green Triangle-Kamp Kanawana Kampers' newsletter (1932-1940), KA-News and Green Triangle issues (1976, 1978-1982), camp brochures, photographs, promotional materials, and t-shirt artwork spanning from the early 1920s through the late 1990s.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (1842-1881) was president of the Montreal YMCA from 1869 to 1870. He was a McGill-educated lawyer and Liberal MP for Argenteuil (1874-75), married Ellen Myra Macdougall in 1869, published the first Cushing family genealogy in 1877, and died March 1, 1881.

Lemuel Cushing Sr. (1806-1875) had 13 children including 8 sons: Colonel James Brock, Lemuel Jr. (1842-1881), Thomas (founded Montreal Brewing 1876), Francis (hired Olmsted), Charles (notary), Frederick (b. 1851), William Mair (d. 1925), and others.

Since Lemuel Cushing Jr. died in 1881, the 'Lemuel Cushing' who led the 1892 YMCA camping trip to Lake Saint-Joseph must be a third-generation Cushing — either a son of Lemuel Jr. or a grandson of Lemuel Sr. bearing the family name. James Stevenson Cushing (1878-1957), author of the 1905 genealogy update, was born in Quebec and is likely a son or close relative of Lemuel Jr.

The motto 'Non Nobis Solum' derives from Cicero's De Officiis (1:22): 'non nobis solum nati sumus ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici' — 'Not for us alone are we born; our country, our friends, have a share in us.' It is itself a translation of a sentiment from Plato.

Lower Canada College (LCC, founded 1909) shares the motto 'Non Nobis Solum' with Camp Kanawana. LCC founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery adopted it from the Fosbery family crest. Whether Kanawana adopted the motto independently or through LCC connection is unknown.

The Pagé family has deep roots in Saint-Sauveur. Boulangerie Pagé was established in 1903; Édouard Pagé acquired it in 1914. 'Domaine-Pagé' is a named locality in Saint-Sauveur. The 'Page family' from whom the YMCA acquired the camp property is almost certainly this Pagé family.

Weredale House (Boys' Home of Montreal) was founded in 1870 by Charles Alexander (1816-1905), a Scottish immigrant confectioner and philanthropist. Alexander built the institution at his own expense on Mountain Street and served as president from 1870 until his death. Over 1,000 boys were housed during his presidency.

Before Camp Weredale (1934), Weredale House boys attended a shared camp in Ste. Marguerite from the 1920s. An earlier 'Camp Boy' was sponsored in 1918, renamed 'Camp Lewis' in 1919 after Major John Lewis, killed in WWI.
Library and Archives Canada holds the Weredale House fonds (1868-1975), containing textual records, graphic material, and architectural drawings.

Dave Twynam (G. David Twynam) was camp director of Kamp Kanawana circa 1979. He later became an academic specializing in outdoor recreation, tourism, and event management — Dean of Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University and previously at Thompson Rivers University.
A Flickr account under the name 'Kanawana' hosts 4,416 photos. The Instagram account (@ymcakanawana) has 571 posts. Neither has been reviewed for historical content.
Camp Kanawana held a 120th anniversary reunion at Victoria Hall on September 5, 2014.
A Montreal Gazette article from February 24, 1933 titled 'Music and Comedy in Fossils' Revue' reveals an alumni group called 'the Fossils' connected to Camp Kanawana.

A Montreal Gazette article from August 5, 1942 titled 'Y.M.C.A. Boys Stage Parade and Circus' names Camp Director R.H. Hanagan (in Indian garb on horseback) and Resident Director E.E. Smee. Mentions Bantam/Junior/Intermediate/Senior sections.
Ross Bannerman authored a 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' in 1969 (Concordia Archives), suggesting a senior role at the camp — possibly director — during that period.
David Leduc managed all Kanawana summer/winter programs (75 employees, 800 participants) per LinkedIn. Dates of service unknown.
Sean Day confirmed as 'former director' of Camp Kanawana (post-2022). Kate Taylor and Kevin Slezak are current leadership.

E.E. Smee held the role of 'Resident Director' at Camp Kanawana in 1942, distinct from the Camp Director role held by R.H. Hanagan. This documents a two-tier directorship structure during the wartime period.
Sean Day grew up at Camp Kanawana, as stated in a 2017 CBC article about the Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund.
Sean Day held the dual title of 'Regional Director of Camps for the Quebec YMCAs' and 'Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana' simultaneously, as confirmed by multiple CBC News articles (2017-2022).

In 2021, Sean Day decided to close Camp Kanawana's overnight camp due to COVID-19, as offering overnight services to 250+ campers was not feasible. YMCA Quebec instead offered 10 day camps (up from 3 the previous summer).

In May 2022, Sean Day reported Camp Kanawana had only hired 75% of counsellors by end of April (normally fully staffed by then). YMCA made 'huge increases' to salaries to recruit staff. Waiting lists existed at many YMCA camps.
After leaving YMCA Quebec (c. April 2023), Sean Day's LinkedIn title is 'Director of Fund Development', and prior KB notes indicate he moved to the Rossy Foundation.
Sean Day said of Camp Kanawana: 'Helping kids to understand their potential in the context of community and nature is what the camp is all about.' (CBC, 2017)

E.E. Smee's full name was Edgar E. Smee. The McMorris thesis lists him as 'Edgar Smee' (Juvenile section director, 1939) and the 1942 Gazette article uses 'E.E. Smee' (Resident Director). These are the same person.

Edgar E. Smee died on February 7, 2002, at the Glebe Centre in Ottawa, at age 89. He was survived by his wife Frieda, daughters Linda, Susan, Sydney, and Sonia, and brothers Norman and Leonard. Obituary published in The Globe and Mail, February 11, 2002.
Edgar E. Smee was born circa 1912-1913 (age 89 at death in February 2002). His hometown was Hamilton, Ontario, where he grew up swimming in Red Hill Creek as a boy.

Edgar E. Smee returned to Hamilton in 1968 after a 30-year absence (c.1938). He was dismayed by pollution at Red Hill Creek and local beaches, which 'sparked a deep anger' and led to his environmental activism.

Edgar E. Smee was the founding Chair of the Conserver Society of Hamilton & District (originally 'Clear Hamilton of Pollution' / CHOP, founded 1969; incorporated as Conserver Society 1984). He helped create the first action plan for Hamilton Harbour/Burlington Bay.

Edgar E. Smee was named Environmentalist of the Year in 1983 (EOY Awards). The Ed Smee Conserver Society Environmental Fund was established in his honour in 1999, managed by Hamilton Community Foundation.

Edgar Smee's 30-year absence from Hamilton (c.1938-1968) aligns with his documented Kanawana service (1939 Juvenile section director, 1942 Resident Director), suggesting he may have been based in Montreal during that period for YMCA work.

G. David Twynam (Dave Twynam) held a faculty position in the School of Outdoor Recreation, Parks, and Tourism at Lakehead University in Thunder Bay, Ontario, as confirmed by his author affiliation on publications from 1998 and 2002.

G. David Twynam became Dean of the School of Tourism at the University College of the Cariboo (UCC), which later became Thompson Rivers University (TRU) in Kamloops, BC. He served as Dean for over a decade.
David Twynam was identified as 'TRU Dean of Tourism' in March 2008 at the Cariboo Skills Competition.
Dr. Dave Twynam departed as Dean of the School of Tourism at TRU around 2009, replaced by Dr. Harold Richins.
After leaving TRU, Dave Twynam became Dean of the Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University (VIU) in Nanaimo, BC.

Dave Twynam received the Transfer & Articulation Community Leadership Award from the BC Council on Admissions and Transfer, nominated unanimously by the BC Tourism Management Articulation Committee. He had served as System Liaison Person (SLP) for the committee for 15 years.
As Dean at TRU, Twynam was involved in the inaugural launch of the Bachelor of Tourism Management program, which was subsequently offered at several other BC post-secondary schools.
Dave Twynam holds a PhD (confirmed by 'Dr.' title in multiple institutional sources and 'Dave Twynam, PhD' on Heart of Gold Project).

G. David Twynam has 10 research works with 723 citations on ResearchGate. Key publications include: (1) Farrell, Johnston & Twynam, 'Volunteer Motivation, Satisfaction, and Management at an Elite Sporting Competition', Journal of Sport Management 12(4), 1998; (2) Johnston, Twynam & Farrell, 'Motivation and Satisfaction of Event Volunteers for a Major Youth Organization', Leisure/Loisir 24(1-2), 1999; (3) Twynam, Farrell & Johnston, 'Leisure and volunteer motivation at a special sporting event', Leisure/Loisir 27, 2002; (4) Johnston & Twynam, WWF Arctic Tourism Guidelines sustainable tourism principles.

Twynam co-developed the Special Event Volunteer Motivation Scale (SEVMS), a 28-item instrument with four factors: Purposive, Solidary, External Traditions, and Commitments. This scale has been widely cited and validated internationally.

Dave Twynam was involved in the Heart of Gold Project, an international sustainability collaboration between VIU/Nanaimo and Costa Rican institutions (Earth University, Cartago University College, Rainforest Alliance of Costa Rica).
Dave Twynam is now retired from VIU. His LinkedIn lists him as 'Retired, former Dean, Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University.'

Twynam's career trajectory: YMCA Camp Kanawana director (~1979) → Lakehead University faculty, School of Outdoor Recreation, Parks & Tourism (by late 1990s) → Dean, School of Tourism, University College of the Cariboo / Thompson Rivers University (~1999-2009) → Dean, Faculty of Management, Vancouver Island University (post-2009) → Retired.

Twynam's academic research on volunteer motivation and special events was conducted at Lakehead University in Thunder Bay, using data from the 1996 Scott Tournament of Hearts (Canadian Women's Curling Championship) and the 1997 Scouts Canada Canadian Jamboree, both held in Thunder Bay.

Twynam's research also includes sustainable tourism (WWF Arctic Tourism Guidelines with M.E. Johnston), marine tourism (HMS Erebus and Terror National Historic Site in Nunavut), and residents' perceptions of sporting event impacts.

Camp Becsies was a YMCA Montreal camp documented in Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12D, with textual records dating from 1929-1936 and 1960-1971 (3 cm of records).
Camp Dorval was a YMCA Montreal camp documented in Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12E, with textual records dating from 1926-1928 (0.5 cm of records).

Camp Perrot was a boys' camp operated by the Montreal YMCA alongside Kamp Kanawana. Concordia Archives hold a 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (c.1945-46) and a further comparison of Kamp Kanawana and Camp Perrot (1953-54).

Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye was a YMCA Montreal canoe-tripping program that began with exploratory trip logs from 1958 and a La Vérendrye Park pilot project proposed budget c.1959. The program leased land at Lac Landron in 1962-63, produced brochures by 1963, and maintained camper records from 1967-1980, with a review booklet in 1982.

The modern YMCA Kanawana Voyageurs program descends from the Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye program (est. 1958-59). Current offerings include: 12-Day Travelers (Voyageurs) paddling the Coulonge, Dumoine, and Noire Rivers; Adventurers Coureurs des Bois (4-6 day introductory canoe trips in La Vérendrye Wildlife Reserve); and 26-Day Voyageurs Ultimate (21-day white water canoe trip).

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A (Committees) holds a 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (c.1945-46), a Boys' Camping Committee Survey Committee report (1950), and a 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' (1974).

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds a 'journal of the first Montreal YMCA venture to explore the country around St. Agathe with the view of securing a lake for a summer camp' dated 1895.

In 1921, Mabel C. Jamieson and Ferna G. Halliday jointly acquired land from Mr. Leguerrier at what would become Camp Ouareau. At the time, Quebec law prohibited women from buying or owning property without their father's or husband's permission; both women had to fight to get their fathers' permission to purchase.

Ferna G. Halliday was a graduate of Queen's University. From 1918 to 1921, she served as secretary of the Christian Association of Young Women (YWCA) of Montreal and was responsible for young girls at Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians.

Mabel C. Jamieson was National Student Secretary of the Christian Association of Young Women of Canada in 1915. After completing her studies in 1918 at Pupils College in Richmond, she became secretary general of the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal at least from 1915 to 1920, and was a member of the Committee of the Sixteen in 1919.

Ferna Halliday co-directed Camp Ouareau in 1922 and 1923. In spring 1922, she toured to Sherbrooke to promote the camp's opening. From 1924, Mabel Jamieson directed Camp Ouareau alone while Halliday founded Camp Oconto in Tichborne, Ontario.

Camp Oconto, an all-girls camp on Eagle Lake in Tichborne, Ontario, was founded by Ferna Halliday in 1924. Halliday ran it each year until 1949 when June Kennedy Labbett and Cliff Labbett took over. Halliday Hall, the original dining hall built in 1924, is named in her honour.

Camp Ouareau and Camp Oconto continued to operate on the same mission with similar traditions, including opening and closing rituals featuring candlelight ceremonies with classical music, poetry, and tableaux.
Dorothy Percival became director of Camp Ouareau in 1934 and acquired the site in 1937. She believed in women's education and paid for some campers to attend school.
Joyce Bertram became manager and owner of Camp Ouareau in 1954, having purchased it from Dorothy Percival. She introduced the camp mascot 'Bymph' and composed several camp songs still sung today.

In 1970, Madeleine Allen created the Language Program at Camp Ouareau, bringing together two aspects of Quebec culture. In 1976, the camp began accepting 50% francophone campers, shifting from an English-only camp.

Jacqui Raill became director of Camp Ouareau in 1994 (she had been a counsellor since 1975). She and her husband Don Raill became co-owners in 2002. Their daughter Gabrielle Raill became assistant director in 2004 and co-director since 2011.

Camp Ouareau's Lodge was built in 1922 and is one of the oldest log buildings still in use in Canada. The camp site covers 14.5 hectares including a peninsula on Leguerrier Bay and two islands on Lac Ouareau.
In May 1941, a forest fire south of Lac Ouareau threatened Camp Ouareau's facilities and its summer opening; the camp was ultimately spared.
In 2014, Camp Ouareau changed its team names from Iroquois, Algonquin, and Micmac, and shifted many names and signs on camp to remove Indigenous-themed naming.
Camp Ouareau (est. 1922) is one of the two oldest summer camps exclusively for young girls still in operation in Canada, alongside Glen Bernard Camp in Huntsville, Ontario (also 1922).
Camp Oolahwan was the longest sustained initiative in YWCA Montreal history. Founded in 1917, it operated until 2005 and contributed to the healthy development of thousands of girls and women.

Mary Susanna Edgar founded Camp Oolahwan in 1917 on Lake Walfred in Sainte-Marguerite-du-Lac-Masson in the Laurentian mountains, north of Montreal. It was an English-speaking camp exclusively for young girls.
The Camp Oolahwan centennial reunion was held in 2017 at Camp Ouareau in Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci. Sources disagree on exact dates: YWCA says September 8-10; West Island Blog says August 25-27.
Ferna Halliday was among the founding members of the Ontario Camping Association in 1933, alongside Mary Edgar, Taylor Statten, Ethel Statten, A.L. Cochrane, and Mary Hamilton.

Montreal's Committee of the Sixteen was formed in 1918 to study 'commercialized vice.' Mabel C. Jamieson was a member in 1919, indicating her involvement in Montreal social reform networks alongside her YMCA and camp work.

Camp Ouareau today serves girls and gender minorities aged 6-16, with capacity of 143 campers per 2-week session and nearly 500 campers per summer. It is divided into three age groups: Nova (6-11), Luna (12-13), and Senior (14-16). The camp operates a bilingual French-English linguistic program.

The YWCA Montreal claims Camp Oolahwan (1917) was the first summer camp for girls in Canada. However, Camp Northway in Ontario predates it (founded 1906). The YWCA claim likely refers to the first YWCA-operated girls camp.
The Canadian Camping Association (CCA/ACC) was founded on May 20, 1936 at the Central YMCA, Toronto.
The first CCA officers were: Taylor Statten (president), Mary Edgar (vice-president), Dr. George S. Patterson (secretary), Mary C. Donaldson (treasurer).
The CCA's primary objective was to 'further the interests and welfare of children, youths and adults through camping as an educative, recreative, and character developing experience.'
The CCA Constitution was incorporated by Letters Patent issued by the Secretary of State for Canada at Ottawa on November 4, 1949.
The Quebec Camping Association (QCA) was formed in 1937 as a chartered unit of the Canadian Camping Association.

Concordia University YMCA archives hold correspondence regarding the founding of the CCA Quebec Section dated 1936-1937, a constitution from 1937, and executive/members meeting records from 1937-1942.
A camping school affiliated with the QCA was held at McGill University from 1937 to 1940.

The CCA published 'Canadian Camping' magazine from 1949 to 1988. Digitized issues are available on archive.org through efforts of Trent University and Joe Richards.

The Centenary Journey (1967) was a CCA/provincial camping association Centennial project where campers paddled a cross-Canada route from coast to coast. Bruce Hodgins was key to the project's success.
Taylor Statten served as ACA (American Camp Association) president in 1942, in addition to being first CCA president.
Mary Edgar (1889-1973) was Director of Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians from 1915-1919 while serving as YWCA Girls' Work Secretary in Montreal.
Camp YMCA Kanawana is an accredited member of the Association des camps du Québec (ACQ), the modern successor to the Quebec Camping Association.
