Kirk Wipper developed comprehensive canoeing standards that were approved by the Ontario Camping Association and used in most camps with canoeing programs.

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds 'History of Camping' notes dated 1936, the same year the CCA was founded.

Camp Kanawana's site is 550 acres with 3 lakes, located in the Laurentians 45 minutes from Montreal.

Sean Day held the dual title of Regional Director of Camps for the Quebec YMCAs and Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana, serving from 2004 to approximately April 2023 (19 years). He grew up at Camp Kanawana and was Matt Aronson's counsellor. After departing YMCA Quebec, he became Director of Fund Development at the Rossy Foundation.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Sean Day made the decision to close Kanawana's overnight program, citing the impossibility of offering overnight services to 250+ campers. The YMCA pivoted to 10 day camps (up from 3 the previous summer). David G. Leduc held a BA in International Development from Dalhousie University and an MBA from McGill (2006-2011). Career sequence: Oxfam-Québec Lebanon coordinator (2000-2002), YMCA Kanawana program manager (dates uncertain, managing 75 employees and 800 participants), McGill ICAN director of operations, Executive Director of Development and Peace (2015-2020), Director of Philanthropy (Quebec) at Pathways to Education.

Ferna G. Halliday, co-founder of Camp Ouareau (1922), was a Queen's University graduate and Secretary of YWCA Montreal (1918-1921) responsible for girls at Camp Oolahwan. She co-directed Camp Ouareau 1922-1923, then founded Camp Oconto in Tichborne, Ontario (1924), running it until 1949. Camp Ouareau land was acquired in 1921 from Mr. Leguerrier, under Quebec law requiring fathers' permission for women to buy property. The camp is located at 2464 Route 125, Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci, on 14.5 hectares of Leguerrier Bay, Lac Ouareau, including a peninsula and two islands.
A. Ross Seaman graduated from Sir George Williams University and subsequently offered a colleague a job at the Cornwall YMCA, indicating early career involvement with the Ontario YMCA network.
A. Ross Seaman served as teacher and chairperson of the Community Recreation and Leadership Training (CRLT) Department at Dawson College from 1974 to 1984.
A. Ross Seaman and his wife Margaret developed the Elder Hostel Program at Concordia University's Loyola Campus after his retirement from Dawson College.
A. Ross Seaman served as acting chair of Concordia University Leisure Studies during the 1986-87 school year (more precise than earlier 'during the 1980s' claim).
A. Ross Seaman's home community was Vankleek Hill, Ontario, where he is remembered for church and community involvement. A scholarship is given in his name from Vankleek Hill Collegiate.

The A. Ross Seaman Memorial Leadership Development Fund hosts an annual awards evening with auction — described as possibly the only active Concordia scholarship that raises funds this way. Awards are presented annually at Dawson College. The fund designation code is ES0042.

Five organizations give scholarships in A. Ross Seaman's name: Dawson College, Concordia University, Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, and Vankleek Hill Collegiate. The Dawson CRLT scholarship is $500 to a second-year student displaying leadership, community service, caring, and concern for others.

The Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund was established by Stuart McLean and his family to help children in need attend Camp Kanawana. McLean returned to Camp Kanawana in 2005 for a week and hosted one of his Vinyl Cafe shows there.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Camp Kanawana was closed for overnight camping for two consecutive summers (2020 and 2021). In 2021, YMCA Quebec chose to run 10 day camps instead of reopening overnight operations. Sean Day said offering overnight services to more than 250 campers at once did not seem possible.

Léontyne Haché began attending Camp Kanawana at age eight and eventually became its canoe and kayak program specialist in summer 2019. Gaëtane Verna attended as a camper, counsellor, and section leader at Camp Kanawana.

Camp Kanawana is described as located 90 kilometres north of Montreal (CBC 2017) and 10 minutes from Saint-Sauveur (YMCA website). These distances suggest the camp is near Piedmont/Saint-Sauveur in the Laurentians.

Taylor Statten's full name was Emerson Taylor Statten (1882-1956).
Taylor Statten's wife was Ethel Page ('Tonakela'), co-founding director of Camp Wapomeo. Their son Taylor Statten II ('Dr. Tay', 1915-2016) took over as Camp Director in 1954.
Taylor Statten mortgaged his home to fund Camp Ahmek's opening in 1921. The camp opened for six weeks with 60 boys living in tents.

The CSET program was formally launched in October 1918 with two tiers: Trail Rangers (ages 12-14) and TUXIS (ages 15-17). A parallel girls' program, Canadian Girls in Training (CGIT), was also created. Based on a 'fourfold' development philosophy: intellectual, physical, spiritual, and social.
Taylor Statten organized the first Ontario TUXIS and Older Boys' Parliament in 1917.

Hedley Dimock and Charles Hendry conducted their pioneering research at Camp Ahmek starting in 1923, published as 'Camping and Character' (1929/1931). William H. Kilpatrick (progressive educator, colleague of John Dewey) wrote the foreword.
Taylor Statten was elected ACA president in 1941 but resigned due to illness; VP Wes Klusmann assumed responsibilities.
The Taylor Statten Camps commissioned 42-foot war canoes from the Peterborough Canoe Company in 1926, reportedly still in use.

The Concordia Archives (P0145/12A) place Hanagan's report alongside: 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (Kanawana and Camp Perrot, c.1945-46), 'Report of the Montreal YMCA Camps for Boys and Girls' (1946), and an ACA Conference report to the Board of Management (1946). This confirms Hanagan's portfolio extended beyond Kanawana.

Howie Langille was Camp Chief/Director in 1941 (48th season, 68 staff, 30+ British wartime evacuees). No director is documented between Langille (1941) and Hanagan (1942), suggesting direct succession.

Dr. Cushing, identified as a pediatrician, visited Kanawana during the 1946 polio outbreak and recommended cancelling canoe trips but keeping the camp open. Three of six cases were discharged by end of summer. This Dr. Cushing is distinct from W.E. Cushing who wrote 'Historical sketches' in 1943.

Derek Walsh (ACQ — Association des camps du Québec) received the CCA Award of Excellence in 1983. The CCA fonds at Trent University Archives associates him with 'Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, Montreal, Quebec.'

The chronology is inconsistent (YWCA role 1915 precedes 1918 studies), suggesting possible source confusion. She was also a member of the Committee of the Sixteen in 1919 and 'made a career in teaching.'

A Montreal Gazette article from July 11, 1918 titled 'At Camp Kanawana' reports a record attendance of 110 campers and mentions filming by visiting YMCA representatives from London.

The name 'Kanawa' used by Kirk Wipper for his canoe museum derives from Proto-Arawak meaning 'dugout canoe' — a South American/Caribbean word that entered English as 'canoe' via Taino/Spanish. It is unrelated to 'Kanawana', which is likely Algonquian in origin.
Dr. James Orbinski received the Pip Alumni Award in 2024. He is known for his work with Doctors Without Borders (MSF).
Dr. Marina Sharpe received the Pip Alumni Award in 2018. She is a refugee law expert.
Camp Kanawana's official Flickr photostream contains 4,416 photos, primarily documenting modern camp life.

A CCA photograph from a 1972 Board of Directors meeting at Montreal City Hall is held in the CCA fonds at Trent University Archives.

Terry Mosher's full name is Christopher Terry Mosher, OC. His pen name 'Aislin' is a rendition of his eldest daughter Aislinn's name (without the second 'n').

Terry Mosher attended fourteen different schools in Montreal, Toronto, and Quebec City. He studied art at Toronto's Central Technical School and the Ontario College of Art, then dropped out to hitchhike across North America for two years. He graduated from the École des Beaux-arts (now part of UQAM) in 1967.

Terry Mosher's first published cartoon was a drawing of Charles de Gaulle in Saturday Night magazine (September 1967). His first newspaper cartoon appeared in the Montreal Star on December 10, 1967. He was appointed official cartoonist of the Montreal Star in 1969.
Terry Mosher has produced more than 14,000 editorial cartoons and approximately 52 books. He co-authored 'The Hecklers: A History of Canadian Political Cartooning' (1978) with Peter Desbarats.

Terry Mosher won the National Newspaper Award in 1977 (cartoon of René Lévesque) and 1978 (cartoon of the new Pope). He was the youngest person inducted into the Canadian News Hall of Fame in 1985 (age 43).
In 1993, MP Robert Layton denounced an Aislin cartoon in the House of Commons, making Terry Mosher the first political cartoonist censured in the House of Commons.

The Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant holds the Guinness World Record (as of 2012) for the longest canoe race in history: 3,283 miles (5,283 km) with 60 miles of portaging across 70 portages.

Gene Rheaume of Flin Flon conceived the Voyageur Canoe Pageant idea in 1963 as a two-man canoe race. Norm Tyson drafted the formal proposal to the Centennial Commission in 1964. Arnie Charbonneau transformed it into a voyageur pageant with larger canoes.

The 10 race canoes for the Voyageur Pageant were built by Moïse Cadorette of St-Jean-de-Piles, Quebec, in fiberglass (~400 lbs each), replacing fragile wood-and-canvas prototypes from Chestnut Canoe Company.

Each Voyageur Pageant canoe was named after an explorer: NWT (Mackenzie), Yukon (Campbell), BC (Fraser), Alberta (Thompson), Saskatchewan (Kelsey), Manitoba (Radisson), Ontario (McGillivray), Quebec (La Vérendrye), NB (Champlain), NS (Cabot).

Team Manitoba captain Norm Crerar and Gib McEachern (both 27) had won the Flin Flon Trout Festival Canoe Derby three times as amateurs and six times as professionals. Nearly the entire team was from Flin Flon.

Bruce Hodgins (1931-2019), Trent University professor and leader of Camp Wanapitei, was an 'extremely active member of the committee that organized the CCA Centenary Journey' in 1967. Hodgins later received the Dorothy Walter Award of Excellence (OCA) and the Jack Pearse Award of Honour (CCA, 2013).

The CCA Centenary Journey was a relay-style educational canoe expedition: campers in every province paddled a section of a cross-Canada route. Planning began April 23, 1964. A book, 'A Log of Canada's Centenary Journey,' was published in 1971.

Several Voyageur Pageant canoes survive: Radisson (Fort Dauphin Museum), Thompson (Rocky Mountain House), Kelsey (Western Development Museum Saskatoon), Champlain (Woodsmen's Museum Boiestown), McGillivray (private, Thunder Bay), Campbell/Mackenzie (BC middle school). Three have been lost.

Misao Dean's 'The Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant as Historical Re-enactment' appeared in Journal of Canadian Studies 40:3 (Fall 2006), pp. 43-67, and was later incorporated into her book 'Inheriting a Canoe Paddle' (U of T Press, 2013).

The YMCA of Montreal was founded November 25, 1851, the first YMCA in North America, predating Boston (December 29, 1851) by about one month. The founding meeting was held at St. Helen Street Baptist Church in Old Montreal.

The YMCA Montreal built purpose-built buildings at: Victoria Square (1873), Dominion Square (1891, reportedly tallest building in the British Empire), and Drummond Street (1912, $540,206 cost). A 500-room residential annex was added to Drummond Street in 1931 during the Great Depression.

Sir George Williams College was organized in 1926 as the education arm of the YMCA of Montreal, named after YMCA founder George Williams. It received a university charter in 1948, becoming Sir George Williams University. On August 24, 1974, SGWU merged with Loyola College to form Concordia University.

The YMCA Montreal was renamed 'Le Y du Québec' around 2009. It now operates as Les YMCA du Québec / The YMCAs of Quebec (ymcaquebec.org). As of 2025 it has 9 centres, 36 service points, serves 120,000+ people, and operates Camp YMCA Kanawana as its sole remaining camp.

The YMCAs of Quebec underwent a major strategic restructuring in November 2019, closing Guy-Favreau and Hochelaga-Maisonneuve centres, shifting toward community programs and away from large fitness facilities. Day camps were discontinued fall 2025; Kanawana summer camp continues.
Pascale Audette was appointed President & CEO of the YMCAs of Quebec in November 2024, the first woman in this role.

J.H. Winn was elected first president of the Montreal YMCA shortly after its 1851 founding. T. James Claxton's father was directly involved in the founding; Claxton chronicled the history in a 1944 letter to G.W. Birks.

The motto 'Non Nobis Solum' is derived from Cicero's De Officiis 1:22 (44 BC), which itself is a Latin translation of a sentiment from Plato's Epistle to Archytas. The full passage reads: 'non nobis solum nati sumus ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici' ('Not for us alone are we born; our country, our friends, have a share in us'). Cicero associates the concept with the Stoic ideal of cosmopolitanism.

Camp Kanawana uses the abbreviated form 'Non Nobis Solum' rather than the full Cicero quotation 'Non Nobis Solum Nati Sumus.' The camp presents the motto trilingually: 'Non Nobis Solum — Not for ourselves alone — Pas seulement pour nous-memes.'

The motto 'Each for all and all for each' (Kanawana's earlier English motto, documented 1922 and 1927) is also the current motto of YMCA Hayo-Went-Ha Camps in Michigan, founded 1904. This suggests the English motto may have been a common YMCA camp motto rather than unique to Kanawana.

Lower Canada College founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery (headmaster 1909-1935) adopted 'Non Nobis Solum' from the Fosbery family crest when he founded the school. The Fosbery family crest motto predates LCC. Fosbery was a Trinity College Dublin graduate in classics.

The Pip Alumni Award is named for Philip 'Pip' Caddell (1913-2004), who was a Kanawana camper in 1928, and his grandson James Caddell (1973-2005), a camper and counsellor from 1983 to 1991 who became a UN Peacekeeper and died of altitude sickness in Bolivia. The award was established in 2007.

The 'Non Nobis Solum' motto is NOT a YMCA-wide motto. It is specific to Camp Kanawana within the YMCA. No other YMCA camp was found using this Latin motto. The Wikipedia list of organizations using it includes schools (Massanutten Academy, Walnut Hill School, Pennthorpe School, LCC, University College Durham, Willamette University, Washburn University, Swarthmore College class of 1918), military units (US Army 1st Maintenance Company), and heraldic families (Baron Haden-Guest).

The word "kanawa" is a widespread Wanderwort in South American and Caribbean languages (Karina kanawa, Trio kanawa, Wayana kanawa, Taino *kanowa) meaning "dugout canoe." This root is widely believed to be the origin of the English word "canoe." Whether the name "Kanawana" derives from this root or from an Algonquian source is unconfirmed.
Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA" from 1974, and "Camping and Outdoor Education planning" for 1974-1975.

Camp Kanawana runs school group programs focused on conservation and nature. EMSB students have participated in overnight experiences learning about modern conservation, nature, and team building, then planning community-based conservation action projects.

The YMCA Camp Kanawana site sits on unceded traditional territory. The Laurentians were historically occupied by the Weskarini Algonquin First Nation. Nearby Mohawk communities include Kanesatake and Kahnawake.

Richard Patten (1942-2021) served as Director of International Programs at the Metropolitan YMCA in Montreal from 1971 to 1976, and as Executive Director of YMCA Montreal from 1976 to 1979. As Executive Director during 1976-79, Patten would have been the senior YMCA official overseeing Camp Kanawana during Dave Twynam's directorship (~1979).

Richard Patten worked in summer day camps for the Montreal YMCA as a young person while attending Sir George Williams University in Montreal. He later worked in different branches of the Y. This places him in YMCA Montreal camping programs in the early-to-mid 1960s.

Richard Patten's family rented a cottage at YMCA Geneva Park on Lake Couchiching every summer, indicating lifelong YMCA affiliation. He served as President of the Canadian Council for International Cooperation.

John Cleghorn (b. July 7, 1941), former Chairman and CEO of Royal Bank of Canada (1994-2001) and Chancellor of Wilfrid Laurier University (1996-2003), is a Camp Kanawana alumnus. Camp Kanawana facilities include: Front Camp (Farmhouse and Blockhouse, winterized), Woodsy section (12 cabins with electricity), Pioneers section (cabins), Coureurs des Bois section (prospector tents), Pathfinders section (prospector tents), Rose des Vents Pavilion (kitchen, wood stove, common area, max 16 people), 14 prospector tents total. Common buildings: cafeteria, gymnasium called Katimavik, arts and crafts pavilion, beach lodge, nature nook.
The gymnasium at Camp Kanawana is named Katimavik.
Lake Wilson nature camp sites offer rustic camping with prospector tents and fire pits. Described as one of the most beautiful parts of the camp site, with views, sunsets, and stargazing.

Hedley G. Dimock (son of Hedley S. Dimock) was Coordinator of Staff Development and Training for the Montreal YMCA and a lecturer in Group Development at Sir George Williams University. He authored multiple research studies conducted at Camp Kanawana including "A Study of the Change in Attitudes and Temperament of Counselors during a Summer in Camp" (1961), "A Study of the Prediction of Success of Twenty-Seven Camp Counselors" (1961), and "Studies on the Affect of Participation in Training and Supervisory Programs" (1969).

Hedley S. Dimock (father) taught at the YMCA College alongside Charles E. Hendry and authored "Administration of the Modern Camp." He was a key figure in the elaboration of social group work within the YMCA system.

Hedley G. Dimock co-authored works with Raye Kass, published by Captus Press. His published books include "Designing and Facilitating Training Programs," "Simplified Guide to Program Evaluation," "Intervention and Empowerment," "How to Observe Your Group," and "Intervention and Collaborative Change."

In summer 2024, the YMCAs of Quebec launched "Kanawana Adventure," a day camp program at the Camp Kanawana site in Saint-Sauveur. This is the first day camp offering at the historically residential camp.

Charles "Smillie" Buckland attended Camp Kanawana starting in 1944 at age 10. He was sent because his mother felt he needed male influence after his father died when he was three. He took the train from Montreal Central Station to Saint-Sauveur, then bused to camp on a gravel road.

Charles "Smillie" Buckland was the first recipient of the Green Triangle award, described as "the coveted Green Triangle awarded to a camper who accomplished a series of feats." He also held the lake swim record.

The Green Triangle award at Camp Kanawana was given to campers who accomplished a series of feats. Charles Buckland was its first recipient circa 1944-1948. The Green Triangle was also the name of the camp newsletter (known issue: July 29, 1938, digitized on Internet Archive).

In 1944, campers traveled to Camp Kanawana by train from Montreal Central Station to Saint-Sauveur, then by bus up a gravel road to the camp. This is a later travel route than the 1922 route via Place Viger Station to Piedmont.

Leigh Evans attended Camp Kanawana for 6 summers: 1 as camper, 1 as Leader-in-Training, and 4 as staff member. She was announced Capitaine for the Voyageur team of the L&V games in 2012. Capitaine is described as "one of the highest honours a staff member can receive."
The L&V (Lumberman and Voyageur) games are described by alumna Leigh Evans as "a 3-day event in which every person, campers and staff alike, unite with their team." Teams are Lumberman and Voyageur.
Camp Kanawana is described with the saying: "If you have never been, you can not understand it and if you have been, you can not explain it." (Leigh Evans blog)

In fall 2025, the YMCAs of Quebec discontinued all day camp programs including Kanawana Adventure (launched 2024) and all holiday/spring break camps. The overnight residential summer camp at Kanawana continues to operate. The decision was described as part of a "simplification process" to "ensure the viability of the organization in the long-term."

Camp Jubilee/Otoreke was located in Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, not in Saint-Sauveur. It was situated on several islands in the middle of a lake with a landing area on the shore. It was renamed from Camp Jubilee to Camp Otoreke in 1909. It closed in 1982 after nearly a century of continuous operation.

The Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Journal of the first Montreal YMCA venture to explore the country round about St. Agathe with the view of securing a lake on which to establish a Summer Camp and journal of Summer Camp 1895" — the earliest documented YMCA camping journal.
The Voyageurs Ultimate program at Camp Kanawana runs from approximately July 20 to August 14 (26 days), for participants aged 15-17.

Kate Taylor is Camp Director of YMCA Camp Kanawana. She appeared on the Go Camp Pro "Beyond Camp" podcast discussing social media advocacy and exploring privilege. She was part of the camp leadership team during COVID-19 alongside Sean Day and Kevin Slezak.

YMCA Kanawana offers a winter experience package (January 6 to March 7) that includes snowshoeing adventure adapted to group skill level, outdoor games, a snack on the campfire, and a raclette and fondue dinner in a warm shelter. Available for families, corporate groups, and other groups. Includes all food and snacks with custom menu.

The Rose des Vents Pavilion at Camp Kanawana is available from October 15 to May 20 in 'refuge mode' (without running water), by reservation only. Maximum capacity 16 people. Includes 3 bedrooms, equipped kitchen with cookware and dishes, wood stove, and common area.

Camp Kanawana has five distinct seasonal rental windows: (1) May 21-June 23: full camp package; (2) June 23-August 20: summer camp in session, limited rental 6-26 persons only; (3) August 20-October 14: full camp package; (4) October 15-May 20: Rose des Vents Pavilion in refuge mode; (5) January 6-March 7: winter experience package with snowshoeing and fondue.

YMCA Quebec runs the C-Vert environmental leadership program for ages 14-16, where youth become eco-citizens through bike trips, weekend camping, environmental workshops, and a remunerated July internship creating a community environmental project. Goals include 'reconnecting urban youth with nature to protect them from nature deficit disorder.' Funded by Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions and Secretariat a la jeunesse du Quebec.

Camp Kanawana aspires to be 'Quebec's environmental education leader,' marrying 'its tradition of YMCA value-based camping with leading-edge programming' according to a Program Specialists job posting by Les YMCA Quebec.

Chris Adam, Coordinator of Sustainability Office at Dawson College (Pip Award 2017), has had a 35-year career including 25 years at Dawson in Community Recreation (CRLT department). He is also Executive Director of Earthvalues Institute, a non-profit using 'Nature as Mentor' philosophy. Under his leadership Dawson achieved AASHE Platinum rating (global first for associate-level institution) and International Green Gown Awards Sustainability Institution of the Year.

A 'Familles en nature: 4 saisons de plaisir' program held an activity at Camp Kanawana in Spring 2013, featuring a forest hike exploring spring flora and fauna followed by canoeing and a campfire dinner.
Camp Kanawana is listed on Bonjour Quebec (Quebec tourism portal) as a 'holiday centre' with operating season May 15 to October 15, 2026.

Sam Lazarus's mother Janet Torge is a Montreal broadcaster and writer. His brother Riel Lazarus is an archivist and researcher for film and TV. They established the Sam Lazarus Fund to send children who couldn't otherwise afford camp to Kanawana.

Camp Kanawana corporate retreat packages for groups of 3+ days include: meeting room for up to 16 people, custom food services, Wi-Fi, projector, flip chart, and projection screen, with lodging in Rose des Vents Pavilion and cabins. Price: $643.75 per person per night.

Camp Kanawana's official Flickr account (flickr.com/photos/kanawana/) contains 4,416 photos. Account joined 2010, has 12 followers. Confirmed as official YMCA camp presence via toutMontreal.com listing.

Lac Kanawana participates in Quebec's Reseau de surveillance volontaire des lacs (RSVL) voluntary lake monitoring network. Monitoring includes Secchi disk transparency every two weeks (June-October) and water samples for phosphorus, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll a analyzed by CEAEQ. Water quality data available from at least 2013.
Meal services at Camp Kanawana are only offered for groups of 75 people or more. Reservation for 3 meals per day is required, and food services are invoiced per person.

Jeniene Phillips Birks (also credited as Jeniene Phillips) was a CBC Montreal television journalist who served as fill-in anchor on CBC Montreal's evening newscast (circa 2009, alongside Andrew Chang, Kim Brunhuber, and Nancy Wood filling in for Michel Godbout). She also has IMDB credits as producer/actress on The Art of War (2000) and The Apprentice: Martha Stewart (2005).

Janet Torge, mother of Sam Lazarus, is a Montreal broadcaster, radio talk-show host, traffic reporter, Montreal Gazette columnist, and author of 'Dear Sam.' She is also co-founder of the first Rape Relief Centre in Canada (1973) and founder of Radical Resthomes.

John Cleghorn chaired the Montreal YMCA and was named Officer of YMCA Canada's Fellowship of Honour. He was drafted by the Toronto Argonauts but declined, having played defensive lineman on McGill Redmen's national championship football team. He served as Chancellor of Wilfrid Laurier University (1996-2003) and is a Companion of the Canadian Business Hall of Fame.

Richard Patten had an extensive YMCA career before entering politics: Director of International Programs, Montreal YMCA (1971-76); Executive Director of the YMCA in Montreal (1976-79); Director of International Programs, Canadian National Council of YMCAs, Ottawa (1979-87). He worked with Palestinian youth in refugee camps (Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Gaza) under UNRWA/World Alliance of YMCAs, trained YMCA staff in Guyana (1969-71), and coordinated support for Ugandan Asian refugees expelled by Idi Amin.

Carol Skinner's full name was Carol Sharman Skinner. She was diagnosed with ALS in 2013. She worked as Director of YMCA Camp Hayward in Cape Cod, Massachusetts; earned a Master's in Art Therapy; served as school counsellor for five years; and worked as Art Therapist for the Canadian Mental Health Association in Ottawa.

Chris Adam founded the Sustainable Happiness Certificate at Dawson College. Under his leadership, Dawson College declared itself carbon neutral and won Sustainability Institution of the Year at the International Green Gown Awards (out of 56 finalists from 19 countries).

James Orbinski attended John XXIII High School in Montreal before Dawson CEGEP. He received the Meritorious Service Cross (1997) for his work during the Rwandan genocide. He received the Concordia University Loyola Medal in 2017.

Marina Sharpe previously served as Senior Legal Officer with UNHCR in Addis Ababa, Postdoctoral Fellow at McGill Law, and lawyer at Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP in New York. She holds a SSHRC Banting Fellowship and is called to the bars of New York and England & Wales.

The 1983 CCA Award of Excellence recipients were: Derek Walsh (ACQ), Rick Ryan (ACQ), Wayne Perkins (ACA — Alberta Camping Association), and Abe Goss (provincial association not confirmed). Two ACQ representatives were honored in the same year.

Janet Torge is a Montreal-based writer and television documentary producer. Her career spans: radio talk-show host, traffic reporter, Montreal Gazette columnist, prenatal teacher and doula, construction site manager, software manual creator, and co-founder of the first Rape Relief Centre in Canada (1973).

Janet Torge is the founder of Radical Resthomes, a co-living housing model for seniors conceived approximately 30 years ago. Inspired by the Baba Yagas feminist community in Paris (heard about in 2011), Radical Resthomes promotes self-directed, affordable housing where residents manage their own community and age in place.

Janet Torge's book 'Dear Sam: Grieving the Death of My Son' was published by iUniverse (ISBN: 9780595423835). The book describes her coping with the death of her son Sam Lazarus through writing letters to him and imagining his responses.
Janet Torge also authored 'I Can't Believe I'm Old: Essays on Aging,' published by Linda Leith Publishing (Montreal).
Janet Torge's television documentary producer credits include: 'Harry Gulkin: Red Dawn on Main Street' (2004), 'The Great War' (2007), and 'The Gig Is Up' (2021).

Janet Torge is a member of the CIHR Institute of Aging Older Adult Advisory Council and is listed as a 'Lived Expertise Advisor' for the Aging in the Right Place (AIRP) initiative at Simon Fraser University.
Janet Torge operates 'Torge Ahead Inc,' a freelance company offering television documentary production, prenatal classes, doula services, and a weekly health radio show.

As of 2015, the Five-Hole Sam Street Hockey Jamboree (Sam Jam) had raised over $260,000 and sent over 70 kids to Camp YMCA Kanawana. The event is organized by Sam's brother Riel Lazarus. Sam was known as a legendary street hockey goalie who let goals through 'the five-hole' (between the legs), inspiring the event name.

The Sam Lazarus Fund continues to operate via the Fondation des YMCA du Québec. As of 2024, the fund accepts donations through Zeffy. Over 17 years, dozens of families have been offered camperships for children from diverse backgrounds.
Janet Torge is listed in the QWF Literary Database of Quebec English-Language Authors and has contributed to POV Magazine (Canada's premiere documentary magazine).

When Camp Oolahwan ceased physical operations in 2005, it was replaced by 'Summer Space Day Camp,' an urban day camp sharing the same objectives of empowering young women through self-confidence, healthy habits, and leadership, but in a city environment rather than a residential camp setting.

Camp Oolahwan's programming focused on developing healthy minds and bodies, encouraging self-esteem, building lasting relationships, adopting healthy life habits, leadership roles, nature protection, learning new skills, sports, and campfire singing. The YWCA stated that since 1915 it believed young women must acquire self-confidence and the ability to 'laugh and have fun.'
The Camp Oolahwan centennial celebration in 2017 was organized by a committee of former campers and counselors. Camp Oolahwan has a Twitter account (@campoolahwan) created for the centennial.

Lac Kanawana's RSVL lake number is 573. Additional physical characteristics: volume 1,273,000 m³, mean depth 5.4 m, altitude 318.4 m, watershed area 5.17 km², drainage ratio 22.00. Associated watershed organization: ABRINORD. A 2013 results sheet ('Fiche de résultats 2013') was produced by CRE Laurentides.

A. Ross Seaman died in 1987. The A. Ross Seaman Memorial Fund was established in 1987 to honour his life-long dedication to the communities of Concordia University, Dawson College, Kamp Kanawana, and the YMCA. Five organizations — Dawson, Concordia, Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, and Vankleek Hill Collegiate — give a scholarship in his memory annually.

A. Ross Seaman was Director of Kamp Kanawana for 'many years.' His earlier career was in community work and the camping movement with the YMCA. In 1963, he was a part-time faculty member in Applied Social Science and an active collaborator in the Centre of Human Relations and Community Studies at Concordia University (then Sir George Williams). After retiring from Dawson in 1984, he served as acting chair of Concordia University Leisure Studies during the 1986-87 school year.

The A. Ross Seaman memorial scholarship at Dawson College is a $500 award presented in the CRLT program each year to a second-year student who displays leadership, community service, caring and a genuine concern for others.

A. Ross Seaman had a connection to Vankleek Hill Collegiate (a high school in Vankleek Hill, Ontario), which is one of the five organizations that gives a scholarship in his memory. This suggests a biographical connection to eastern Ontario/Prescott-Russell region.
The Concordia University Archives hold photographs of 'R. H. Dawson' (likely Ralph H. Dawson) and R. L. Charlton (undated) in the YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145/12A.
Camp Kanawana staff receive over 80 hours of training. The camp is described as 'a founding member of the Association des camps du Québec (ACQ)' and 'renowned for its high standards of supervision.'

A Camp Kanawana staff member (unnamed) began in the camp industry in 1996, started integrating the summer camp management team in 2002, and served as director of expeditions at Kanawana from 2007 to 2010.

Camp Kanawana's staff career progression ladder includes: Junior Counsellor → Counsellor → Section Director → Canoe Guide → Camping Programs Coordinator → Summer Camp Assistant Director. A program director role (all Kanawana) was filled in 2024.

Camp Weredale was NOT a YMCA camp. It was established in 1934 by the Rotary Club of Westmount, which bought 260 acres with a mile of shoreline on Lac l'Achigan (55 miles north of Montreal) and gave the property to Weredale House (formerly Boys' Home of Montreal). The camp served orphaned and at-risk boys from Weredale House.

Camp Weredale remains operational today, owned and operated by the Weredale Foundation. Located on Lac l'Achigan in the Laurentians, it welcomes 4 cohorts of 85 campers (340 total) from late June to mid-August, serving boys and girls aged 6-17 receiving youth protected social services or facing family challenges. The camp celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024.

Weredale House (Boys' Home of Montreal) was founded in 1870 by Charles Alexander, a Montreal confectioner from Dundee, Scotland. In the 1920s the Rotary Club of Montreal raised $289,000 to build a new Boys' Home. Library and Archives Canada hold the Weredale House fonds: bylaws/annual reports (1887-1971), minutes (1868-1971), registers (1881-1975), Camp Lewis/Weredale records (1919-1966). Camp Weredale suffered a fire and was reconstructed in 1965.

A commenter on the Westmount Magazine 2017 Stuart McLean tribute identifies themselves as the Camp Kanawana director who worked with McLean as assistant director in the summers of 1974 and 1975. The commenter also sublet McLean's Dorchester apartment and looked after his piano when McLean moved to Toronto. The commenter's name is not extracted from the search snippet.

Stuart McLean's connection to Camp YMCA Kanawana dates back to the summer of 1969. He spent five summers at camp in the late 60s and early 70s, beginning as a counsellor in the senior boys' section and working up to assistant director. He passed up a chance to study journalism at Carleton University to return to camp as assistant director. He also served as a student services coordinator at Dawson College in Westmount.

Wilson Griffith McConnell (1908-1966) was a jazz collector who amassed a collection of music recordings and recording equipment. His collection was donated to Concordia University Libraries' Special Collections by his widow Marjorie Wallace McConnell in 1994 and 2000.

The Fong biography of J.W. McConnell (2008) contains Chapter Six titled 'Keep the Home Fires Burning: Fundraising for the YMCA in Peace and for Canada in the Great War, 1909-19' starting at page 123. The book is 733 pages. The full text is behind paywalls (JSTOR, De Gruyter) but available for borrowing on Internet Archive.

The McGill University Archives hold the J.W. McConnell Fonds (MG4240) with series including: 1) Correspondence, 2) Scrapbooks/Journals/Address books, 3) Personal and Family records, 4) Philanthropy, 5) High society, 6) Business Commitments. Series 4 includes subseries on Hospitals/Health Care, Higher Education, and War Efforts. Some files (containers 11-13, 15-17) are restricted.
Wilson Griffith McConnell and his wife Marjorie Wallace McConnell had one daughter, Jill.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (1842-1881), who was YMCA Montreal president 1869-70, published 'The Genealogy of the Cushing Family' in Montreal in 1877. He died at age 39 in Montreal and could NOT have been the 'Lemuel Cushing' who brought boys to Lake Saint-Joseph in 1892. The 1892 Cushing must be a third-generation Lemuel or a nephew. A supplement to the genealogy covering 1905-1969 was compiled by James Stevenson Cushing (born 1878).

The Cushing genealogy (1905 supplement by James Stevenson Cushing, published in Montreal by Perrault Printing Co.) is digitized on Internet Archive but blocked by proxy. A physical or VPN-accessible copy would identify the 1892 'Lemuel Cushing' who brought boys to Lake Saint-Joseph. The rootsweb.com Cushing genealogy index and seekingmyroots.com files may also contain this information.

H.B. Cushing assisted in the founding of the Children's Memorial Hospital (now Montreal Children's Hospital) in 1902-1904, alongside A.D. Blackader and with encouragement from Sir William Osler. This externally confirms that Harold Beveridge Cushing (b. 1873, M.D. McGill 1898) was the same H.B. Cushing described in the 1905 Cushing genealogy as 'Physician to Children's Hospital.' The Children's Memorial Hospital opened January 30, 1904 on Guy Street in Montreal.

Robertson Macaulay Cushing, son of Charles Cushing and Lily Margaret Macaulay Cushing of Montreal, was killed in WWI and is buried at Nine Elms British Cemetery near Ypres, Belgium. He appears on the McGill Honour Roll 1914-1918 and Page 585 of the First World War Book of Remembrance. His wife was Mabel Louise Dawson Cushing of Montreal. This confirms Charles Cushing (Lemuel Sr.'s son, the notary) had children active in Montreal into the WWI era.

Lydia Maria Cushing, one of Lemuel Sr.'s daughters, married into the Beveridge family (married name: Beveridge). This is the likely origin of the middle name 'Beveridge' given to Harold Beveridge Cushing (b. 1873), son of Lemuel Jr. — named after his aunt's married family.

J.W. McConnell (1877-1963) led a massive YMCA fundraising campaign in 1909, raising $320,000 in a single 12-day campaign. Upon first arriving in Montreal he had roomed at the YMCA, which 'nurtured a lifelong commitment to that organization.' William Fong's biography 'J.W. McConnell: Financier, Philanthropist, Patriot' (McGill-Queen's UP, 2008) dedicates Chapter 6 to 'Fundraising for the YMCA in Peace and for Canada in the Great War, 1909-19.'

The McConnell Foundation describes its relationship with Camp Kanawana as 'long' and states it is 'proud to have contributed to Camp Kanawana over the years.' Recent funding contributes to the YMCA 'Springboard for Life' campaign supporting major renovations at Camp Kanawana, honouring the camp's 'long relationship with the Foundation.'

The YMCA chapter of William Fong's J.W. McConnell biography (2008) is titled 'Keep the Home Fires Burning: Fundraising for the YMCA in Peace and for Canada in the Great War, 1909–19', covering McConnell's YMCA fundraising from 1909 through the First World War.

A Lac Wilson in Sainte-Lucie-des-Laurentides (Commission de toponymie du Québec fiche no_seq 135620) is officially recorded as named for the owner of the lands where the lake is located, a person named Wilson — a documented example of the Quebec pattern of Wilson-named lakes referencing local landowners.
Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, the municipality adjacent to the Kanawana site, has 96 bodies of water, including lakes Marois, Ouimet, Guindon, Johanne, Suzanne, Parent, and des Seigneurs.

A. Ross Seaman died in October 1987. The Concordia Applied Human Sciences funding page describes his death as 'a loss to countless people from many places where he expended his energies and warmth to help others to become the best they could be.'

Search-engine snippets of the Concordia 12B01 finding aid (retrieved 2026-06-11, two independent queries) describe correspondence from 'Camp director Dave Twynam' dated 1976, which if accurate would extend his directorship back to 1976. An earlier extraction of the same finding aid (f_0752) dated such correspondence to 1979. Whether the finding aid lists two separate correspondence files (1976 and 1979) or one of the datings is an error is unresolved.

Canada's fourth polio epidemic wave ran from 1946 through 1953 and became the country's most serious, ultimately involving all provinces and reaching into parts of the Arctic. During polio outbreaks, summer camps, playgrounds, pools, and youth centres were commonly closed.

Thomas Cushing (entry 881, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 15 April 1843, married Margaret Ellen Cameron of Lachute on 7 January 1874, and was President and Manager of the Montreal Brewing Co. as of 1905. Sons: Thomas Hubert (b. 1877) and Gordon Cameron (b. 1880); first son Archibald Ronald Cameron died in infancy.

Charles Cushing (entry 883, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 1 May 1848, graduated McGill B.C.L. 1869, practised as a Notary-Public in Montreal, married Lily M. Macaulay (daughter of Robertson Macaulay) on 28 January 1883, and was elected a Director of Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada in 1904. His seven children included Robertson Macaulay Cushing (b. 22 June 1884).

William Mair Cushing (entry 884, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 25 October 1853; Captain of the 6th Fusiliers, Montreal (1878) and later Captain of the 11th Argenteuil Rangers; removed to Elkhorn, Manitoba in 1884, serving as Councillor and Reeve for 8 years.

George Cushing (entry 885, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 2 April 1857; travelled the Western States, worked mines at La Trinidad, Otaez, Mexico, and as of 1905 resided in Mexico City as managing director of the Canada Mexico Trading Co.

James Brock Cushing (entry 878, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 2 October 1839 and died at his residence 'Ingleside', Cushing (Township of Chatham), Que., 22 October 1903. He resided at Cushing until October 1890, when he moved with his family to Montreal; in February 1900 he returned to Chatham as Superintendent of the Carillon and Grenville Canals. For many years he was Colonel of the 11th Battalion (Argenteuil Rangers), retiring as Lieut.-Colonel with the long service and Fenian raid service medals. His son James Wilfred (b. 13 July 1874) died 6 October 1892; son Lemuel (b. 26 November 1875) became a chartered accountant.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (entry 880, 1905 genealogy): born Chatham, Que., 18 February 1842; McGill B.A. 1865, B.C.L. 1865, M.A. 1867, LL.D. 1879; admitted to the Quebec Bar November 1865; Liberal MP for Argenteuil; President of the Montreal Lacrosse Club and an original member of the Montreal Amateur Athletic Association; 'at one time President' of the Young Men's Christian Association; published the first Genealogy of the Cushing Family in 1877; died in Montreal 1 March 1881.

The 1905 Cushing genealogy gives two different birth dates for Lemuel Cushing Sr.: the child listing under Job Cushing (entry 525 reference) says 29 April 1806, while his full entry says 26 April 1806 (both at Three Rivers). Internal discrepancy in the primary source; possibly an OCR or typesetting error.

In January 2009, the YMCA du Grand Montréal and its 8 regional branches took the name 'Ys du Québec' — the organization now operating as Les YMCA du Québec / The YMCAs of Quebec. The organization was previously named YMCA du Grand Montréal.

Per the Observatoire de l'action humanitaire YMCA history: in 2008 the organization decided to build a new centre in Montreal's Ahuntsic-Cartierville borough, and renovations at Camp Kanawana between 2007 and 2009 were undertaken as part of the YMCA du Québec's commitment to sustainable development and environmental respect.

The Concordia AtoM finding aid lists 'Montreal YMCA Camping Branch Board of Management records — 1969-1970', documenting that by 1969 camping was governed by a dedicated Camping Branch with its own Board of Management (succeeded in records by the Camping and Outdoor Education Branch, 1972-1979).

Camp Y Kanawana's 'virage vert' (green shift) began in 2006. All buildings renovated or constructed at the camp since 2006 were energy-efficient and incorporated educational elements, with the goal of reducing the camp's ecological footprint and making it an outdoor education centre focused on environmental education.

In February 2009, Les Y du Québec announced a new phase of the Camp Y Kanawana revitalization plan involving construction of new accommodation facilities. Environmental features documented in the March 3, 2009 Mediaterre article include green sanitary installations, thermal (heat) exchangers, composting toilets, and an artificial wetland system (marais artificiel) for treating wastewater.
Camp YMCA Kanawana's Facebook page hosted a video titled 'Sean Day against Bullying — Message from our Director Sean Day!', documenting Day's public anti-bullying advocacy as camp director.

The YMCA's proposed Kanawana-Weredale two-site operation (planning documents 1977-1980) coincided exactly with the institutional dissolution of Weredale House: the residence closed in 1977, the year its parent merged with Summerhill Homes, the Girls' Cottage School, and Allencroft Reception Centres to form Youth Horizons. The timing suggests the two-site plan arose from (or was complicated by) this upheaval in Weredale's governance, though no source states why the plan was abandoned.

Per the 1935 camp history, the final week of camp began with an 'eating-out day, when every camper went over to the haunted house and cooked his own supper.' The same day, the dam which had kept the water in Lakes Kanawana and Wilson 'at a desirable height' was let out before the assembled campers. The 'haunted house' was thus an established camp-wide cookout destination within walking distance of camp, not merely a story setting.

The Chopsy legend as told in oral tradition: In the summer of 1945, a kitchen staff member named Charles de Grandprix, a WWI veteran who was very skilled with knives and nicknamed 'Chopsy,' was walking in the woods when he found two Senior boys who had snuck off to practice throwing axes stolen from the Hike and Trip Department's equipment room ('the Cave'). He hid behind the tree they were throwing at, intending to scare them. After hearing two axes hit the tree he jumped out, not realizing there was a third ax, which severed his arm. He grabbed the severed arm, put it in his satchel, and fled into the woods. The camp searched but could not find him and declared him dead.

The Chopsy legend continues: Over the following winter, strange occurrences happened at camp. The next spring, boys on a hike found a makeshift cabin in the woods and a car stolen from a nearby town, parked between trees in a way that it could not be driven out. During the summer, dead animals were found in the woods appearing to have been mauled. A solitary senior boy who had been warned not to go into the woods alone disappeared. A search was launched but nothing was found. A counselor checked the car — the trunk, previously open, was now locked. They broke it open and found the missing boy's body, killed with an ax. The body was still warm. Chopsy was never seen again, but for years people claimed to hear chopping sounds deep in the woods late at night.
The full Chopsy legend takes approximately one hour to tell in complete detail. The story was known to campers in the early 2000s era (Matt Aronson's time).
Chopsy's real name in the legend is Charles de Grandprix. He was described as a WWI veteran and kitchen staff member who was very skilled with knives, which is how he earned the nickname 'Chopsy.'
The Hike and Trip Department at Camp Kanawana had an equipment room known as 'the Cave.' In the Chopsy legend, axes were stolen from this room by senior boys.

The Chopsy legend shares several elements with the American 'Cropsey' camp-legend archetype (a disfigured figure haunting the woods near camp, an origin story involving an accident, a weapon) but is a distinct, fully developed narrative with named characters, a specific year (1945), a three-act structure, and details unique to Kanawana (the Cave, kitchen staff, WWI veteran backstory, the locked car trunk, the warm body, the chopping-sounds coda).

The Chopsy legend was traditionally told at the wreckage of an old car in the woods near an abandoned cabin. The car is known as 'Chopsy's Car' and the cabin was known as 'Chopsy's Cabin.' The cabin has since been destroyed. The physical car and cabin served as both the setting of the story's climax and the venue for its telling.

The Chopsy legend traditionally opens with an oral tradition chain formula: 'I'm going to tell you a story my counsellor told me, and that he said his counsellor told him, his counsellor's counsellor told his counsellor, and that they say has been passed down just like this since the summer it happened, right here, at Camp Kanawana... It began in the summer of 1945...' This framing explicitly presents the story as an inherited tradition passed counsellor-to-counsellor, anchors it to the physical camp site, and positions the listener within the chain of transmission.

At least one teller of the Chopsy legend (Matt Aronson, 2000s era) added to the opening formula: 'and I've looked it up in the Kanawana archives at Concordia, and it's all documented there... you can go check and see for yourself...' This embellishment references the real Concordia University Archives (YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145) to lend verisimilitude to the legend.

The dining hall Grace at Camp Kanawana was not a single fixed prayer but rotated among several sung graces. Two identified graces are: (1) 'Johnny Appleseed' (the folk grace 'Oh, the Lord is good to me, and so I thank the Lord...'), and (2) the lyrics of 'Joy to the World' by Three Dog Night ('Jeremiah was a bullfrog...') adapted as a grace. Multiple graces were used rather than the same one at every meal.

The Kanawana Marching Song/Cheer as performed in the 2000s era opens with a call-and-response: the Chief shushes the crowd ('Shhh, shhh, shhh...'), calls 'Kamp Kanawana, are you ready?!', the camp responds 'We are!', and the Chief says 'Then let's go!' The main body begins with 'Hail, Hail, the gang's all here / What the heck do we care, what the heck? / We're the guys from Kanawana / We're gonna sing our marching song-a!' followed by 'We're gonna shout, shout, shout like anything / And through the woods we're gonna yell...' It ends with a coda: 'Ringle, wrangle, jingle, jangle / What's the matter with the Green Triangle? / Sis-boom-ba-ha, Sis-boom-ba-ha / Kanawana, Kanawana, Rah-rah-rah! / K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A / K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A / YEAH!'

The Kanawana Marching Song/Cheer references the 'Green Triangle' in the coda ('What's the matter with the Green Triangle?'). The Green Triangle was the camp's identity symbol and the name of its newsletter (1932–1940). The cheer also opens with 'Hail, Hail, the gang's all here,' borrowing from the 1917 popular song of that title (melody from Gilbert & Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance).

Grand Portage was one of the oldest cabins at Camp Kanawana, built sometime after the Lookout (a pre-existing structure on site before Kanawana was founded), the Dining Hall (1911), and the Infirmary (1920s?). It was situated just north of the Senior Parking Lot, to the west of the dining hall.
Grand Portage served as the CIT (Counsellor-in-Training) director's cabin in the 1980s and 1990s.
According to oral history, the end of World War II was heard on the radio at Grand Portage cabin at Camp Kanawana.
The Lookout is a structure at Camp Kanawana that pre-existed the camp's founding — it was on the site before Kanawana was established. It is described as the oldest structure on the property.

Grand Portage cabin was demolished around 2006 to make way for the new washroom buildings constructed as part of the green shift / Clivus Multrum composting toilet installation. The new washroom buildings bear the Grand Portage name.

The Longhouse was a large 2- or 3-story pavilion/boathouse on the Boating Waterfront (due south of the Dining Hall), right at the shoreline of Lake Kanawana. It was used for large group gatherings and dances. The Boating Director (at one point called 'the Admiral') had their living quarters in it.
The Longhouse was demolished by controlled fire around 1979 because it was in an irreparable condition.
The Boating Director at Camp Kanawana was at one point known by the title 'the Admiral.'

According to oral history, 'Lac Desjardins' was the original name of the lake that became Lake Wilson. It was renamed after being bought and donated to the camp (by J.W. McConnell, per earlier oral history). This would explain why no 'Lac Desjardins' appears in current toponymy records — the name was replaced.

According to oral history, Lake Kanawana was originally called 'Lac St Joseph.' The informant subsequently agreed this is most likely a conflation with the 1894 founding site — Camp Jubilee was established at Lake Saint-Joseph near Quebec City in 1894, a different location from the current Saint-Sauveur site (acquired 1910). This claim is likely erroneous.

No building was known as 'the haunted house' in the 2000s era at Camp Kanawana. The identity of the 1935 'haunted house' is unknown to the informant. Other minor ghost stories besides Chopsy circulated but have not yet been documented.

Matt Aronson (2000s-era counsellor) wrote an elaborate creative backstory for the Chopsy character, expanding the legend with historically grounded fiction. In this backstory, Charles de Grandprix's father Louis came from Kahnawake ('Khanawake') and his grandfather was a voyageur for the Hudson's Bay Company. Charles grew up destitute in Montreal's Old Port after his mother died in childbirth and his father drank himself to death (New Year's Day, 1910). He enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces in August 1914, lying about his age. At the Second Battle of Ypres, his Ross Mark II rifle jammed and he killed enemy soldiers with a hatchet. He became feared for hand-to-hand combat in No Man's Land patrols, wielding first a bayonet, then a kitchen knife. The Germans called him 'Der Hirsch Schlachter' (the Stag Slaughterer), but it was his fellow troops who gave him the nickname 'Chopsy.' He was eventually captured and spent the rest of the war as a POW.

The Chopsy backstory written by Matt Aronson represents a modern creative elaboration of the camp legend by an active teller — a piece of camp cultural production that demonstrates how the legend continued to develop through individual storytellers adding historically grounded fiction (CEF enlistment, Second Battle of Ypres, the Ross rifle, No Man's Land patrols) and tying the character's origins to Kahnawake, echoing the documented Kanawana/Kahnawá:ke name connection.

The dam ceremony (opening the dam between Lakes Kanawana and Wilson) was no longer practiced by the mid-1980s. An informant whose camp experience began around 1985 was not aware of the tradition, establishing a terminus ante quem: the ceremony ended sometime between 1935 (last documented) and ~1985.

The Council Ring is located in the far west end of the camp, a 10-15 minute walk past the Senior Boys section. It remains an important ceremonial site in the 2000s era. It hosts the Opening Campfire for each session, the opening campfire of the L&V Games, and the Closing Fire of the summer.

The Council Ring has a tradition of burning a 'time capsule' containing the summer's record of important people, events, and moments at the Closing Fire, then digging it up to read at the following year's Opening Fire. This tradition is believed to be very old, possibly dating to the 1920s or 1930s.

The Council Ring is large enough to seat the entire camp (200+ people) on log benches made from trees from the site, set in three rows around a large central fire bowl made of stones from the site. The bonfires are massive — sometimes 10-12 feet of firewood stacked, with flames reaching 15-20 feet high. The area above the fire pit is kept clear of tree branches.

The section system at Camp Kanawana remained essentially the same from the informant's era (1980s-2000s) through to the present day, confirming the 1959 section names (Pioneers, Woodsmen, Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders) have remained in continuous use for over 60 years.

Magloire Pagé (1826-1901) was a pioneer settler of Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts. He was part of the 10th generation of the Pagé family since their arrival in New France. He married Adéline Beauchamp (1830-1898) on July 28, 1851, in Saint-Jérôme. In the 1885 census, the couple owned lot 43 in the concession of côte Saint-Elmire, Saint-Sauveur.

Magloire Pagé fils (b. 1853, Saint-Sauveur), son of Magloire Pagé and Adéline Beauchamp, acquired the paternal land in 1874 and married Olivine Desjardins on August 3, 1875. Olivine died at age 54 on June 20, 1904, and was buried in the Saint-Sauveur cemetery. Their known children include Léonie Pagé (1882-1941) and Édouard Pagé (b. March 30, 1893).

Édouard Pagé (b. March 30, 1893, Saint-Sauveur), son of Magloire Pagé fils and Olivine Desjardins, began an apprenticeship in baking in 1910 under Ubald Gauthier on Drolet Street, Montreal. In 1912, baker Camille Gauvreau ceded his Saint-Sauveur bakery to his son Ovila, who rented it to Édouard Pagé. Pagé acquired the business in 1914. The bakery (Boulangerie Pagé) has operated continuously at 7 avenue de l'Église since 1903 (when Gauvreau founded it). In 1963, Édouard sold the business to his sons Bernard and Philippe Pagé.

Édouard Pagé served as president of the Saint-Sauveur School Commission (Commission scolaire). His efforts led to the construction of a boys' school that was blessed on January 9, 1949, and named École Saint-Édouard in his honor. The school retained this name until 1995.

Télesphore Pagé, the youngest son of Magloire Pagé fils, married on May 27, 1925, inherited the family land, and settled there with his wife Clarilda Dagenais (1901-1995). The old Pagé farmhouse faced the mountains near Saint-Sauveur.

In 1957, Mickey Stein was staying in the old Pagé family farmhouse near Saint-Sauveur when he observed the mountain opposite and conceived the idea for the Mont Habitant ski resort. With associates Stephen and Stanley Vineberg, Stein developed the mountain, hiring designer Sel Hannah; Mont Habitant opened for the 1958-59 winter season.

The Pagé family genealogy in Saint-Sauveur spans at least four generations: (1) Magloire Pagé père (1826-1901), married Adéline Beauchamp 1851; (2) Magloire Pagé fils (b. 1853), married Olivine Desjardins 1875; (3) children including Léonie (1882-1941), Édouard (b. 1893), and Télesphore (youngest son, married 1925); (4) Édouard's sons Bernard and Philippe (took over bakery 1963). The family owned land on lot 43, côte Saint-Elmire, and 'Domaine-Pagé' is a named locality in Saint-Sauveur whose toponymic origin the Commission de toponymie has not formally determined.

The first bakery in Saint-Sauveur was established in 1897 (not 1903) by Camille Gauvreau, who purchased land from notary Malo. It was later known as the 'Ancienne boulangerie Gauvreau' and is listed in the Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec (ID 206587). The building is at 7 avenue de l'Église, the same location as Boulangerie Pagé. The '1903' date sometimes cited may refer to a different milestone or error; Gauvreau established it in 1897 and Édouard Pagé took it over in 1912-1914.

The YMCA 'Torch Ceremony for World Friendship' originated at a 1926 international YMCA conference where representatives from 52 nations gathered to discuss YMCA involvement in post-WWI peace-building. On the final night, they lit a 'Fire of Friendship' and senior leaders passed torches to the younger generation, who declared in their own languages: 'We leave this fire with a vision of a great Christian fellowship, conscious of difference but resolved to love.' One torch was housed at the Greater Des Moines Y Camp for 99 years. YMCA Camp Fuller (Providence) held a 'World-Wide Friendship' ceremony in 1932 where boys carved sticks with friends' autographs and pledged friendship. Kanawana's 1935 'Torch Ceremony for World Friendship' was part of this YMCA-wide interwar peace tradition.

Dr. James Orbinski is described as 'the 15th recipient' of the Pip Award on the YMCA Quebec press release (2024). With 12 documented recipients through 2018 and Orbinski as the 15th in 2024, exactly 3 awards were given in the 2019-2023 period, while 2 years had no award (likely 2020 and 2021 due to COVID). The 2010 gap is confirmed by numbering: Mosher was the 8th recipient in 2015, meaning one skip year in 2007-2014, which is 2010.

Stuart McLean attended Lower Canada College for high school before becoming a counsellor at Camp Kanawana in 1969. Both institutions use the motto 'Non Nobis Solum.' McLean is the only documented individual known to have attended both LCC and Kanawana, making him a confirmed personal bridge between the two institutions. However, no documented evidence exists of a deliberate motto adoption pathway from LCC to Kanawana.

M.H. Penton authored 'Non Nobis Solum: The History of Lower Canada College' (1972), a history of the school that may contain references to YMCA or camp connections. The book is listed on Internet Archive but has not been accessed. LCC founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery adopted 'Non Nobis Solum' from his family crest when the school opened in 1909.
